TGA is there because it is how cels leave most Japanese paint software. Recommended reader: the `image` crate, MIT or Apache-2.0, default features off and only `bmp`, `tga`, `tiff`, `webp` and `jpeg` on, about twelve new crates, all to go through the Q-04 licence record before they ship. Every one is read as 8-bit sRGB with straight alpha, as a PNG is; a format with no alpha is opaque; a grey file is grey in all three channels. The rule is one sentence: **a drawing in another format is the same picture as its PNG twin** (FX-FMT-001 to 010). The files and the twins are written by Pillow, not by the library the build would use. Formats that keep every value must match exactly; JPEG and lossy WebP must match within 3 of 255, because two correct decoders may round differently. A file the reader cannot read is the existing missing-or-unreadable media diagnostic, no new one. **Out, GIF.** Recommended writer: the `gif` and `color_quant` crates, MIT or Apache-2.0. A GIF has 256 colours a frame and alpha that is on or off, so it is a preview format and the dialog says so. A GIF counts time in hundredths of a second, which 24 frames a second does not divide into, so frame `n` is shown from `floor(n * 100 * den / num)` to `floor((n + 1) * 100 * den / num)` and the delays differ by one so the total never drifts (FX-FMT-020 to 023), as ADR-018 did for samples. **Out, animated PNG.** The `png` crate already in the build writes it: lossless, full alpha, no new dependency. Its frame delay is a fraction, so it is the frame rate's denominator over its numerator and exact. **Out, MP4.** H.264 video in an MP4, no sound (D-71's ceiling stands). The timescale is the frame rate's numerator and every frame lasts the denominator, so 24000/1001 is exact (FX-FMT-030). H.264 needs even width and height: an odd composition is refused before any file is written, with a sentence naming the odd side; nothing is padded or cropped silently. Recommended encoder: the one Windows carries, Media Foundation, reached through the `windows` crate already in the tree through Tauri. The binary then ships no codec of its own, which is the smallest answer to D-30's licence question, and the cost is that MP4 export is Windows only. The other roads, for the owner to weigh: a system `ffmpeg` found at run time (nothing shipped, but the owner must install it); the `openh264` crate (Cisco pays the patent fee only for its own downloaded binary, not for one built from source); WebCodecs in the window (the WebView's encoder, but frames must cross into the page and back). **This is an engineering reading, not a legal opinion, and which road is the owner's to choose under D-30.** Evidence basis: `Fixtures/formats/` from `tools/formats_reference.py`; document 25 shows the tables. Ceilings, stated: 8 bits only for the new drawing formats (16-bit TIFF was to be read down to 8, and said so; **amended by the owner on 2026-09-19, "keep the refusal": a file deeper than 8 bits is refused with MEDIA_UNSUPPORTED_FORMAT, as a 16-bit PNG is, and nothing is read down**); no animated GIF or WebP as a drawing sequence; GIF uses one palette a frame with no dithering choice; no sound in any export; no ProRes, WebM or HEVC. Consequence if accepted: an output-format field on `ExportRequest`, one module per writer beside `src/png_out.rs`, the new crates in the licence record, and the import and relink dialogs list the new extensions. **Found while building B-21d on 2026-09-19, the agent's engineering decisions, none of which changes a fixture.** (1) Media Foundation writes its own clock, 23976 ticks a second with frames of 1000 for 24000/1001, which is not FX-FMT-030; the build rewrites the time numbers in the finished file's index (`mvhd`, `tkhd`, `mdhd`, `stts`) in place and at the same size, and fails the export with a sentence if the index holds anything it does not expect. (2) Media Foundation converts colour with BT.601's numbers and does not label the file, so the build converts to BT.709 itself and hands the encoder NV12; the file still carries no BT.709 label, which players assume at HD sizes and may not below about 720 lines. (3) The Baseline profile, because High adds a table of reordered times (`ctts`) the clock step would have to rewrite. (4) One bitrate rule, 0.2 bits a pixel a frame between 1 and 100 megabits a second, and no quality choice in the window. All four are ceilings on `verification/B-21d_mp4_playtest.md`.

D-73 / Export choices: three MP4 qualities, GIF dithering, the MP4's colour label, and the list says which files are lossless / PROPOSED on 2026-09-19 by the agent as B-22a, with its fixtures first, at the owner's word ("write D-73") after they asked for "a raw export of gif/mp4/animated png and selectable levels of compression/bitrate and color space" and for a recommendation. **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-19 by the owner ("accept D-73, proceed with B-22b and B-22c").** It was written that nothing is built against it until the owner accepts it. **Raw.** A lossless export already exists for everything that can have one: the PNG sequence and the animated PNG keep every value, and EXR is the full-precision master. A GIF cannot be raw, because 256 colours a frame is the format; H.264 through the encoder Windows carries has no lossless mode. So no "raw" choice is added; the list beside Export says which entries are lossless. **MP4 quality.** Three named levels, Preview, Standard and High: 0.1, 0.2 and 0.5 bits for every pixel of every frame, floored to whole bits a second and kept between 1 and 100 megabits (FX-FMT-040). Standard is what B-21d writes today. Flat cel colour is where a low bitrate shows blocks, which is what High is for. No free number box: a number nobody can judge invites films that look wrong with no sentence to explain why. The same rule on both D-30 roads. What the fixture holds is the number asked of the encoder; the size of the file depends on the picture and is not a fixture. **GIF dithering.** One choice, on or off, off being what B-21c writes today. On is Floyd and Steinberg's error diffusion in whole numbers, so that two programs agree to the pixel: a see-through pixel takes no error and passes none on; ties go to the first palette colour (FX-FMT-050 to 052, on fixed small palettes, because the palette `color_quant` picks cannot be reproduced by an independent program). One palette for the whole film, which flickers less, is left until the owner sees flicker. **Animated PNG compression.** Not offered: it changes the file's size and the export's time and never the picture. **Colour space.** No choice. BT.709 in video range is the right answer for HD video, and full range or BT.601 mostly make films that look wrong in someone's player. What is added is the label: the file says BT.709 primaries, transfer and matrix, video range (FX-FMT-060), read back from the H.264 header or the container's colour box, whichever the road writes. That removes B-21d's stated ceiling for compositions under about 720 lines; the ffmpeg road (B-21e) already writes it. Display P3 and Rec.2020 need colour management through the whole program and are not an export choice. Evidence basis: `Fixtures/formats/expected_formats.json`, the new cases from `tools/formats_reference.py`; document 25 shows the tables. Existing cases are unchanged. Ceilings, stated: three levels and no number; one dither method; High stays on H.264's Baseline profile on the Windows road. Consequence if accepted: a quality and a dither field on `ExportRequest`, two more lists in the window shown only for the format they belong to, B-22b the core and B-22c the window.

D-73a / GIF dithering: the carried error is held within limits, to end the coloured specks / PROPOSED on 2026-09-19 by the agent, with its fixtures first, at the owner's word ("B-22c playtest passes; write the D-73 amendment for the specks"). **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-19 by the owner ("accept D-73a, proceed with B-22d")**; FX-FMT-050 to 052 are retired by it and stay in the fixture file, marked so, as the record of D-73's first rule. It was written that nothing is built against it until the owner accepts it. **What was seen.** D-73's dithering passes on the whole difference between the colour wanted and the colour spent. Where the 256 colours have nothing near (the dark trunk, the deep pink of the tree, the grey of the cloud), the difference builds up pixel after pixel until it is large enough to land on a far, bright colour: red dots in the pink, yellow in the trunk, orange in the cloud. **The amendment, two steps added to the rule and nothing else changed.** One: the pixel plus its carried error is held within 0 to 255 before the nearest colour is looked for. Two: the difference is held within plus and minus 16, in each of red, green and blue, before it is shared out 7, 3, 5 and 1 sixteenths. See-through pixels, ties and the flooring are as D-73 has them. **Why 16.** The agent tried the rule in Python on a piece of a real frame of the reference shot, with the 248 colours `plain.gif` uses: `verification/D-73a proposal/as_accepted_against_proposed.png`, D-73 on the left, this on the right. Counting pixels that land further than 80 (of 255, straight-line distance in red, green and blue) from the colour they should be: 805 as accepted; 190 with step one alone; 46 with a limit of 32; none with 16. The sky's bands stay gone at 16. This is the agent's trial, not the build, and one frame of one shot. **What it gives up, stated.** With only a few far-apart colours to spend, dithering can no longer mix them: a mid grey in black and white alone would come out one flat colour, not a checker. A GIF from this program always has up to 256 colours picked from the picture itself, so that case does not arise in an export; it is exactly what FX-FMT-050 to 052 test, so on acceptance those three are retired and FX-FMT-053 to 055 replace them. A large area of a colour the palette lacks becomes its nearest colour, flat, instead of that colour with bright dots (FX-FMT-055 shows both). Evidence basis: `Fixtures/formats/expected_formats.json`, cases FX-FMT-053 to 055 from `tools/formats_reference.py`, insertions only; document 25 shows them. Consequence if accepted: B-22d, a few lines in `dither_indices`, the table walks 053 to 055 in place of 050 to 052, a new `dithered.gif` and side-by-side picture for the owner's eye. No change to the window.

D-74 / Solid layers: a layer that is a rectangle of one colour / PROPOSED on 2026-09-19 by the agent as B-23a, with its fixtures first, at the owner's word ("go, yes to all three; proceed with B-23a"). **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-19 by the owner ("accept D-74, proceed with B-23b")**; B-23b builds it in the core. It was written that nothing is built against it until the owner accepts it. **The layer.** A new layer kind, `solid`, whose drawing is a rectangle of one colour, as After Effects' solid is. It has no `asset_id`, no exposures and no source offset. It carries a `solid` record of three things: `color`, three numbers from 0 to 1, red, green and blue in the working space (linear, as the tint effect's colour is); `width` and `height`, whole numbers of pixels from 1 to 8192. Everything else a drawing has it has, and it means the same: name, switch, lock, in and out frames, transform, opacity, mask, matte (it can shape another layer and be shaped by one), parent, depth, label, shy, blend mode (all of them, unlike an adjustment layer) and its effect stack. The colour and size are not animated. **Its picture.** Document 21's step 1 for a solid is not a decode: it is `width` by `height` pixels, every one the colour, opaque, in its own layer space with (0, 0) at its top left. Steps 2 to 7 then run on it exactly as on a drawing: the mask and the effects in its own space, then the transform, parent and camera, matte, opacity and blend. So a solid and an opaque drawing of the same colour and size give the same frame. **A new solid** is the size of the composition, with its anchor at its own centre and its position at the composition's centre, so it covers the frame exactly, and is named `Solid 1`, `Solid 2` and so on. Changing its size keeps its anchor at the same fraction of its width and height, so a centred solid stays centred, and is one step of history. **The colour in the window** is chosen with the system's colour picker, which works in the 256 levels of the screen: the choice is turned into linear by document 21's sRGB curve and stored so, and the picker shows the stored colour by the same curve back. A colour written into a file by hand in between two of the 256 levels is kept exactly and drawn exactly; the picker shows the nearest level. **Refused.** A file whose solid names an asset, has exposures or a source offset, has no `solid` record, has a colour that is not three numbers from 0 to 1, or a width or height that is not a whole number from 1 to 8192, is `PROJECT_SCHEMA_INVALID`, and so is any other kind of layer carrying a `solid` record (FX-SOL-020 to 029). No build writes any of them. **Commands.** `layer.add_solid`, above the chosen layer or else at the front, Ctrl+Y as in After Effects, with an optional colour, width and height; `solid.set`, the colour, width and height of one solid, one step of history. Both refuse a value outside the ranges above with `COMMAND_INVALID_VALUE`, in a sentence. **Nothing to fetch.** A solid has no media: it is never missing, collecting a package has nothing of it to copy, and it draws the same on every machine. **Ceiling, stated.** A solid is drawn whole, as a drawing is: one of 8192 by 8192 takes a gigabyte while it is drawn. After Effects allows 30000; 8192 is twice a 4K frame each way. Evidence basis: `Fixtures/solid/`, FX-SOL-001 to 008 (frames) and 020 to 029 (refusals), from `tools/solid_reference.py`, which renders each pixel from document 21 and moves by whole pixels only; document 25 shows them. Consequence if accepted: B-23b, the kind in the core and the file, its picture, the refusals and the two commands, with a table that walks FX-SOL-001 to 029; B-23c, the window: New Solid in the Layer menu, the colour and size in the layer's panel, and a playtest sheet.

D-75 / Masks and shape layers: the owner's direction / ACCEPTED as direction on 2026-09-19 by the owner ("go, yes to all three; proceed with B-23a"), the three questions put to the owner after B-22d. It sets what B-24 and B-25 will specify; each still comes as its own rule with its fixtures before code, for the owner's acceptance. **One: shape layers are in, narrowly.** Document 04 kept vector animation out of every stage. It is amended for one thing: a shape layer, after B-24, holding one or several shapes - rectangle, ellipse and paths drawn with the pen - each with a fill and a stroke. Out at first: gradients, trim paths, repeaters and merge paths. The drawing engine stays out; a shape layer is not a paint program. **Two: feather is even first.** A mask's feather is one number, the same all round its edge, softened with the Gaussian blur's own weights. After Effects' point-by-point feather (the variable-width feather tool) comes later, as its own unit. **Three: mask modes.** Each mask has a mode: Add, Subtract, Intersect, Difference or None, applied first to last as in After Effects. **B-24, masks, as planned with the owner:** paths with curves, drawn with the pen, where every polygon mask a file has today keeps its pixels exactly; several masks on a layer, each with its mode, invert, opacity, feather and expansion; the mask path animated. In the window: the pen, rectangle and ellipse tools, moving points and handles, and the masks as rows under the layer in the timeline with stopwatches. Split as B-24a the rule and its fixtures, B-24b the core, B-24c still masks in the window, B-24d animated paths.

D-76 / A solid's colour and size over time / DECLINED on 2026-09-23 by the owner ("i agree with not keyframing it"), after B-24 and B-25 were done, as the recommendation below asked. D-74 stands: a solid's colour, width and height are not keyed. A size over time is Scale keyed, or a shape layer's rectangle with its path keyed (D-78), which keeps a hard edge in pixels. A colour over time has no stand-in yet, for a solid or a shape's fill and stroke alike; if the owner wants one, it is a new decision covering both, with its fixtures first. PROPOSED on 2026-09-19 by the agent, from the owner's question at the B-23c playtest ("have width and height be drag click as well, maybe keyframeable?"). The drag was window work and is built; keying is not, because D-74 says in as many words that a solid's colour and size are not animated, and that is what the file, the schema and `Fixtures/solid` were written to. **Nothing is built against this until the owner accepts it.** **What it would mean.** `color`, `width` and `height` would stop being three plain values in the `solid` record and become three of document 19's properties, each with a base and its own keys, drawn on the timeline with a stopwatch like Position and Opacity. **What follows.** The file changes shape, so every project written since B-23b would be read by a rule that takes the old shape as a base with no keys (no fidelity is lost, but the conversion has to be written down and walked in a table). The picture would be made afresh on every frame where the size changes, so a solid stops being one buffer held still and becomes a decode-sized cost per frame; a keyed size of thousands of pixels is a gigabyte a frame by D-74's own ceiling. The anchor rule ("the anchor keeps the same fraction of the size") is a rule about one change; over time it becomes a question the owner has to answer, because an anchor that is itself keyed cannot also be carried along by the size. **The cheaper half.** Scale is already keyable and already does what a growing rectangle looks like: a solid at a fixed size with its Scale keyed grows and shrinks on screen, with no new file shape, no new cost and no new rule, and it is what After Effects animators reach for. A keyed `width` differs from a keyed Scale in one visible way: the edge stays hard and the number is in pixels of the finished frame rather than a percentage. A keyed colour has no such stand-in; a tint effect with a keyed colour over a white solid is the nearest, and is what the effect stack is for. **What the agent recommends.** Not now: keep D-74 as it is, and revisit after B-24 and B-25 (masks and shapes, D-75), because a shape layer with an animated fill is the same wish and the one After Effects answers with. If the owner wants it anyway, it comes as its own rule with its fixtures before code: FX-SOL-040 upward, a keyed colour, a keyed size, and an old file read into the new shape. Evidence basis: D-74, document 19's property record, and B-23b's cost note. Consequence if accepted: a B-23d of its own, ahead of B-24.

D-77 / What a mask is, from B-24 on / ACCEPTED on 2026-09-19 by the owner ("accept D-77, proceed with B-24b, along with shortcut for the pen tool"), proposed the same day by the agent as B-24a, from D-75. B-24b builds it in the core on 2026-09-19: `verification/B-24b_mask_table.md`. **The shape in the file.** A layer's `mask` becomes `masks`, a list, in the order they are drawn, first to last. Each holds a `name` ("Mask 1", "Mask 2" and so on), `enabled`, `inverted`, a `mode` of `add`, `subtract`, `intersect`, `difference` or `none`, an `opacity` from 0 to 1, a `feather_px` of 0 or more, an `expansion_px` from -8192 to 8192, and a `path`. The path is a document 19 property from the start - `{"base": {"points": [...]}, "keyframes": []}` - so that B-24d only has to fit a stopwatch to it and the file never changes shape twice. A point is `{"point": [x, y], "in": [dx, dy], "out": [dx, dy]}`: the two handles are offsets in pixels from the point, which is D-53's convention for a path, and a handle of `[0, 0]` means no handle. A mask is closed by definition, as document 19 already says; open paths are B-25's business, not a mask's. **What is kept exactly.** A segment whose two handles are both zero is one straight line, and an expansion of zero touches no distance arithmetic at all, so every mask written before this decision draws pixel for pixel what it draws today: same 4x4 grid, same even-odd rule, same sixteenths, ADR-016 unamended. FX-MSK-001 is that claim as a fixture. A file with the old single `mask` key is read as one mask, mode Add, opacity 1, feather 0, expansion 0, every handle zero, `enabled` and `inverted` as it held them, named "Mask 1" (FX-MSK-002); saving writes `masks` and no `mask` key, so a project saved by this build and opened by one older than it loses its mask - which is why a file holding both keys is `PROJECT_SCHEMA_INVALID` rather than a guess (FX-MSK-020). **The curve.** A curved segment is a cubic Bezier through the two points and the two handles, flattened into `n` straight pieces at equal steps of t before the sampler ever sees it, where `n` is the control polygon's length in pixels halved and rounded up, held between 16 and 512, the length summed point, out handle, in handle, point in that order so the count is the same on every machine. Flattening before sampling is what keeps one rasterization rule in the build instead of two. Known ceiling: a curve longer than about 1024 pixels is flattened to pieces of more than 2 pixels and will show it; raising the 512 is an amendment to this decision and changes every fixture it touches. **One mask's own coverage, in this order.** Expansion first: a sample point is inside when its distance to the outline, signed positive within, plus the expansion is zero or more, so a corner rounds off exactly as After Effects rounds one, and a negative expansion shrinks. Then feather: document 21's Gaussian on the coverage alone, separable, normalised, radius `ceil(3 * sigma)`, with `sigma = feather_px / 2`, so a feather of 4 pixels is a band of about 4 pixels; the coverage outside the frame is worked out like any other coverage rather than invented, so a mask against the frame's edge does not darken. Then invert, which is `1 - m`. Then opacity, which multiplies. **Several masks.** The accumulated coverage starts at nothing, except that a first mask in Subtract or Intersect starts from the whole layer, because there would otherwise be nothing to take away from and such a mask could only ever give an empty frame - this is what After Effects does and what an animator expects. Then, first to last: Add is `a + m - a*m`, Subtract is `a * (1 - m)`, Intersect is `a * m`, Difference is `a + m - 2*a*m`, each held within 0 and 1. A mask in mode None takes no part in the picture at all; it is there to be drawn on screen and pointed at. A layer with no mask that takes part is whole, as it is today. **What is kept and diagnosed rather than refused.** A mask of fewer than three points, or one whose points cross, is kept in the file, takes no part in the picture and raises `MASK_INVALID_OUTLINE`, exactly as today (FX-MSK-018, 019); document 28 asks for that rather than losing a project over one bad outline. The crossing test is on the points alone, as it is today - handles are not tested, and a curve that crosses itself is drawn by the even-odd rule, which is defined for it. Known ceiling: the test stays the O(n^2) pair scan `src/mask.rs` already carries its own note about. **What is refused whole**, as `PROJECT_SCHEMA_INVALID`: both keys at once, an unknown mode, an opacity outside 0 to 1, a feather below 0, an expansion past 8192, a point or handle that is not two numbers, a mask with no path, a `masks` key that is not a list, masks on an audio layer (D-71, unchanged), and a keyed path whose key holds a different number of points from its base. That last is the animated-path rule stated now and built in B-24d: a path is interpolated point by point, point and both handles, between keys that hold the same number of points, by document 20's curves; adding or removing a point on a keyed path is a command's problem, not a file's (D-79 is that command, from 2026-09-22; the file rule here is unchanged). **Where it sits.** Document 21 step 2 is unchanged in place and in space: the masks are applied to the layer's own picture, in layer space, before the effects and before the transform, the accumulated coverage multiplying premultiplied RGB and alpha together. Masks are still not inherited through parenting. **What it costs.** Feather is a blur of the coverage field over the layer's own bounds plus the blur radius, per mask, per frame; expansion needs the distance to the outline at every sample, which is the flattened outline's length times sixteen samples a pixel, and is the expensive half of this decision. Both are named here so that B-24b's table can record them rather than discover them. **Evidence.** `tools/mask_reference.py` and `Fixtures/masks/`: FX-MSK-001 to 019 frames within 1e-6, FX-MSK-020 to 030 refused; drawn in `verification/B-24a proposal/mask_cases.png`. Consequence if accepted: B-24b the core, B-24c the window, B-24d animated paths, and document 19, the schema and ADR-016's surrounding prose amended to match at B-24b.

D-78 / What a shape layer is, from B-25 on / ACCEPTED on 2026-09-20 by the owner ("accept D-78, proceed with B-25b"), proposed the same day by the agent as B-25a with its fixtures first, from D-75's first direction. Built in the core at B-25b; the window is B-25c. **The layer.** A new layer kind, `shape`, whose drawing is a list of shapes it carries rather than a file on disk. It has no `asset_id`, no `exposure_spans` and no `source_offset_frames`. **It has no width and no height of its own either**, unlike a solid: a shape layer's space is its composition's space, the same size and the same origin, and it starts empty, transparent black, with the shapes drawn into it. That is what After Effects does, and it means a shape drawn at a place on the picture stays at that place, with nothing to keep in step and no second size to type, key or refuse. Everything else a drawing has it has, and it means the same: name, switch, lock, in and out frames, transform, opacity, masks, matte (it can shape another layer and be shaped by one), parent, depth, label, shy, blend mode and its effect stack. A new shape layer is anchored at the composition's centre and positioned there, so it sits over the frame exactly, and is named "Shape Layer 1", "Shape Layer 2" and so on. **A shape.** A layer holds `shapes`, a list, in the order they were drawn, first to last. Each holds a `name` ("Shape 1", "Shape 2" and so on), `enabled`, a `closed` flag, a `path`, an optional `fill` and an optional `stroke`. The path is exactly a mask's path, D-77's record unchanged - `{"base": {"points": [...]}, "keyframes": []}`, a point being `{"point": [x, y], "in": [dx, dy], "out": [dx, dy]}` with the handles offsets in pixels - so a shape is drawn with the same pen, rectangle and ellipse the mask tools already are, flattened by the same rule, and moves between keys by the same rule, point by point, the point and both handles, through document 20's curves. What is new is that a shape's path may be open: `closed` false means the last point is not joined to the first. **A fill** is `{"color": [r, g, b], "opacity": 0 to 1}`, the colour three numbers from 0 to 1 in the working space, as a solid's is. An open path is closed for the purpose of filling it, by a straight line from its last point to its first, which is what After Effects does. **A stroke** is `{"color": [r, g, b], "opacity": 0 to 1, "width_px": above 0 and up to 8192}`, centred on the path, half its width either side. A shape with neither is kept and draws nothing: that is a path a person has drawn and not yet decided about, not a fault. **Rectangles and ellipses are stored as their points**, the four-point box and the four-segment ellipse the mask tools already make, and not as a width, a height and a roundness. Ceiling, stated plainly: that means there is no Size or Roundness to type or to key, a rectangle whose points have been dragged is no longer a rectangle to anything but the eye, and giving a shape parameters later is an amendment to this decision that changes how every shape is stored. **Its picture, in this order.** Document 21's step 1 for a shape layer is the composition's width by its height in transparent black. Then each shape in the list, first to last, so a later shape covers an earlier one: its fill, then its stroke over its own fill. Coverage is ADR-016's rule and nothing else - the same 4 by 4 ordered grid, the same sixteenths, the same tie-break where a sample on the line counts as inside - so a shape's edge is the same quantum a mask's edge has always been. A sample is inside the fill by the even-odd rule. A sample is inside the stroke when its distance to the flattened path is `width_px / 2` or less. Each of those two coverages, multiplied by its own opacity, composites its colour over what the layer holds so far by document 21's normal blend in premultiplied linear RGBA. Steps 2 to 7 then run on the finished layer exactly as on a decoded drawing: its masks and its effects in its own space, then transform, parent and camera, matte, opacity and blend. So a shape layer can be masked, and a shape is not a mask. **Why the stroke is defined by distance.** Naming the stroke as every point within half a width of the path defines joins and caps without enumerating them: they come out round, because that is what the definition says, and the build needs no offset curve, no mitre arithmetic and no second rasterization rule. It also reuses what D-77 already pays for, the distance from a sample to a flattened outline that mask expansion needs. Ceiling, stated: **joins and caps are round, and only round.** Mitre, bevel, butt and square are out at first, and each is an amendment to this decision that changes every stroke fixture. **A shape may cross itself**, and this is a deliberate difference from a mask. A mask whose points cross is kept, takes no part and raises `MASK_INVALID_OUTLINE`, because nobody can say which side of a crossed mask should be kept. The even-odd rule does say what a crossed shape fills, a five-pointed star drawn in one stroke is the ordinary way to draw one, and so a crossing shape is drawn rather than diagnosed. **Kept and diagnosed rather than refused**: a shape whose path holds fewer than two points cannot be stroked or filled; it is kept in the file, takes no part in the picture and raises `SHAPE_INVALID_OUTLINE`, a new identifier in document 28's table, WARNING on a load and ERROR on a command, which is what that document asks for rather than losing a project over one bad shape. **Refused whole**, as `PROJECT_SCHEMA_INVALID`: a shape layer carrying an asset, exposures or a source offset; a `shapes` key that is not a list; a shape with no path; a `closed` that is not true or false; a point or handle that is not two numbers; a fill or stroke colour that is not three numbers from 0 to 1; an opacity outside 0 to 1; a stroke width that is not above 0 and at most 8192; a keyed path whose key holds a different number of points from its base, as D-77 already refuses; shapes on an audio layer; and any other kind of layer carrying a `shapes` key. No build writes any of them. **What moves and what does not.** The path moves, because it is D-77's property and B-24d already moves it. The colours, the opacities and the stroke width do not, at first, and for the same reason D-76 is open for a solid's colour: each is a property record's worth of work and a stopwatch in the panel, and it is the owner's call whether it is worth a unit. Adding or removing a point on a path that has keys was refused at B-25b, as it was for a mask; D-79 lifts that for both from 2026-09-22, by the same two commands, and changes nothing else written here. **Commands**, each one step of history, each mirroring a mask command that exists: `layer.add_shape`, a new empty shape layer above the chosen layer or else at the front; `shape.add`, a path drawn with the pen, the rectangle or the ellipse on a shape layer; `shape.set_path`, a point or handle moved; `shape.set`, the name, the switch, the fill and the stroke; `shape.delete`; and `shape.add_remove_key` for the path's stopwatch. The tools are B-24c's tools: which of a mask and a shape the pen draws is decided by the kind of layer chosen, so the window gains no third pen. Each refuses a value outside the ranges above with `COMMAND_INVALID_VALUE`, in a sentence. **Nothing to fetch.** A shape layer has no media: it is never missing, collecting a package has nothing of it to copy, and it draws the same on every machine. **What it costs.** A fill costs what a mask of the same outline costs. A stroke costs the distance from every sample to every flattened segment, which is the outline's pieces times sixteen samples a pixel over the layer's bounds - the same arithmetic as a mask's expansion and the same expensive half. Both are named here so that B-25b's table records them rather than discovers them. Evidence basis: `Fixtures/shapes/`, FX-SHP-001 to 017 (frames) and 020 to 030 (refusals), from `tools/shape_reference.py`, which samples each outline from ADR-016's grid and renders each pixel from document 21, written from this rule rather than from `src/`; document 25 shows them, `verification/B-25a proposal/shape_cases.png` draws the sixteen still ones and `verification/B-25a proposal/shape_moving_case.png` draws FX-SHP-017's moving path frame by frame across its row. Consequence if accepted: B-25b, the kind, the shapes, the file and the commands in the core, with a table that walks FX-SHP-001 to 030; B-25c, the window: New shape layer, the pen, rectangle and ellipse pointed at a shape layer, the fill and stroke in the layer's panel, and a playtest sheet; document 04's exclusion narrowed again, documents 19, 21, 24 and 28, ADR-016's surrounding prose and the schema amended to match at B-25b.

D-79 / A point added to or taken off a path that has keys / **ACCEPTED as direction on 2026-09-22 by the owner ("also tackle said limits"), written by the agent as B-24h the same day**, from the two limits B-24d's playtest sheet wrote down. It is recorded here rather than put for acceptance first because it changes no file shape, no schema, no command's refusals and no expected value in `Fixtures/`: D-77 already said in as many words that adding or removing a point on a keyed path is a command's problem, not a file's, and this is that command. **What it does.** A point added to a path is added to the base and to every key at the same place along the same segment, in one command; a point taken off comes off the base and off every key at the same index, in one command. So the agreement D-77 rests on - every key holds as many points as the base - is never broken, not even for an instant, and the rule that refuses a file whose key holds a different number of points from its base is untouched and still refuses one. The same two commands serve a mask and a shape (D-78), because a shape's path is a mask's path. **Where the new point goes.** The segment is cut by de Casteljau's construction at a fraction `t` of the way along it: the cut point is the curve's own point at `t`, its two handles are the two halves of the construction, and the handle on each side is shortened to what that half needs. **Nothing moves.** Both the cut and document 20's interpolation between keys are affine in the control points, so cutting and then interpolating gives the same curve as interpolating and then cutting: the shape at every key is where it was, and so is the shape at every frame between two keys. That is checked against document 19's cubic written out a second time, at two hundred places along every segment, and agrees to about 1e-14 of a pixel. **A straight segment gets a corner.** D-77 says a segment whose two handles are both zero is one straight line; a cut of such a segment puts a corner on the line, with no handles on it and none grown on its neighbours, so a square stays a square with five corners instead of quietly becoming five curves. Ceiling, stated: document 19's cubic walks a handle-less segment by `3u^2 - 2u^3` rather than evenly, so cutting one changes *when* the line is walked, never where it goes - the new point is on the line, but it is not at `t` of the distance along it. **What the pixels do.** The curve does not move, but the drawing of it can, by one thing: `flatten` cuts a curve into pieces about two pixels long, and two short curves are not cut at the same places as one long one. A straight segment cut moves not one pixel; a curved one is measured at 5 pixels of 3072 differing by 0.0625 of full coverage - one of the sixteen samples ADR-016 takes in a pixel - which is the ceiling written into the fixture. **Refused, in a sentence, as `COMMAND_INVALID_VALUE`:** a segment or a point the path has not got, and a `t` that is not more than 0 and less than 1. A mask taken below three points is kept and diagnosed as `MASK_INVALID_OUTLINE`, by D-77's existing rule, unchanged. **The second limit, the same unit.** Every mask edit in the history read "Set mask of N points", whatever it was, because the core takes the whole list of masks as one command. An entry now says what changed, worked out by comparing the list as it was with the list as it is at the moment the entry is made - "Add a point to Mask 1", "Move a point of Face at frame 6", "Set Mask 1's feather to 6 px", "Rename Mask 1 to Face" - so the name comes from the change itself rather than from anything the window says about itself, and a window that sends the same command by another route still gets the right entry. No command gains a field and no file changes. **Evidence.** `tests/b24h_path_points.rs` to `verification/B-24h_path_point_table.md`, which walks the curve, the keys, the pixels, the refusals, a save and reopen, and nineteen history entries; the window's half in `verification/B-24h_panel_table.md`; the owner's sheet `verification/B-24h_path_point_playtest.md`. No new file in `Fixtures/`: nothing this decision does changes a rendered frame that `Fixtures/masks` does not already pin, and the claim being made is an equality between before and after, which is what that table checks. Consequence: B-24h, and the two limits struck from `verification/B-24d_mask_playtest.md`.

D-80 / Several mask points at once, and After Effects' bezier gestures / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-23 by the owner ("proceed with what you personally recommend", against the agent's recommendation to accept it whole, rebinding included), proposed the same day by the agent**, from the owner's word at the B-24f playtest ("I want to multi-select mask points, and be able to drag select as well. also I would like to be able to do bezier curves with these when I click and drag to modify curve amount, etc. make it 1 to 1 with AE's mask ecosystem"). **Nothing is built against this until the owner accepts it**, for one reason only: it takes a gesture the build already has, Alt and a click, and gives it a different job, and the owner has already been handed a sheet that describes the old one. **It changes no file and no fixture.** A point's two handles have been in D-77's record since the first day - `in` and `out`, offsets in pixels, `[0, 0]` for none - and every gesture below writes points and handles through `mask.set_path` and `shape.set_path`, which exist. Which points are chosen is the window's own state, saved nowhere, as a chosen layer is saved nowhere. **What "chosen" becomes.** Exactly one point or one handle is lit at a time today. It becomes a set, on one mask at a time: a click on a point chooses that point alone; **Shift** and a click adds it, or takes it out if it was already in; a click on a mask's outline away from any point chooses **every** point of it, which is how a whole mask is picked up in After Effects; a **box dragged across the picture** while a mask is chosen chooses every point inside it and Shift adds them to what is chosen; Escape or a click on the empty picture clears the set. The same box dragged when no mask is chosen still selects layers exactly as W-06 built it, so nothing that works today stops working. **What acts on the whole set.** A drag on any chosen point moves every chosen point by the same offset, one entry in the history; Shift during that drag holds it to one line, as a layer's drag already is; the arrow keys nudge every chosen point, a pixel a press and ten with Shift; **Delete** takes every chosen point off, in one entry. A handle still acts on its own point alone, as it does in After Effects. **The bezier rules, as After Effects has them.** A vertex is a corner or it is smooth. Smooth means its two handles are kept in line through the point: dragging one turns the other to stay in line and leaves the other's own length alone. Corner means the two are independent and either may be zero, which is every point the pen draws today. **The pen pulls handles out.** Pressing to place a point and dragging before letting go pulls a mirrored pair of handles out of it, which is how any bezier pen behaves and is the thing the owner asked for by name ("click and drag to modify curve amount"); today the pen can only ever place corners, so nothing drawn with it can be curved at all until a handle exists to drag. **Alt converts.** Alt and a click on a vertex makes a smooth one a corner and takes its handles off; Alt, a press and a drag on a corner pulls a mirrored pair out of it and makes it smooth. That is After Effects' Convert Vertex, which is what Alt over a vertex means there. **Alt breaks.** Alt and a drag on a handle breaks the pair: that handle moves alone and its vertex becomes a corner carrying two independent handles. **The pen adds and deletes.** With the pen chosen, the pointer over a segment adds a point there on a click and over a vertex takes that vertex off - After Effects' Add Vertex and Delete Vertex, without a second tool to choose. Those are `path.add_point` and `path.remove_point` exactly as B-24h built them; only the gesture that sends them changes. **The cost of going 1 to 1, stated plainly.** B-24h, on 2026-09-22, bound **Alt and a click** with the selection tool to adding and removing a point. After Effects does not: Alt over a vertex converts it there, and adding and deleting are the pen's hover. Accepting this rewrites steps 1, 2, 3, 7 and 8 of `verification/B-24h_path_point_playtest.md` before the owner ever walks it - which is the cheapest moment to change a gesture, and the reason this is asked now rather than after. The keyboard route built beside it, **+** and **-** on a point that has been tabbed to, is untouched and still answers document 05's keyboard bar; converting and breaking need no key of their own, because both write handles through `set_path`, which the arrow keys already reach. **The core's only half.** Delete with several points chosen would otherwise be one entry of history per point. `path.remove_point`'s `at` accepts several indices separated by commas, taken off from the highest down so the lower ones keep meaning what they meant, in one command and one entry - "Remove 3 points from Mask 1". Nothing else outside the window changes. A list holding an index the path has not got is refused in a sentence as one is today; a mask taken below three points is kept and diagnosed `MASK_INVALID_OUTLINE` by D-77's rule, unchanged. **What is deferred, named rather than left to be assumed**, because "1 to 1 with After Effects' mask ecosystem" is larger than this: the free transform box a double-click puts around a mask, which scales and turns the whole mask by its corners (B-24k, proposed in document 15 and not in this decision); RotoBezier, a path whose curves the program works out and which has no handles to drag; the Mask Feather tool and point-by-point feather, which document 15 already defers; Mask Interpolation and Smart Mask; the Mask Shape dialog that types a mask's bounds as numbers; and mask tracking. None is needed by anything above, and each is a unit or an amendment of its own. **Evidence if accepted.** `tests/b24h_path_points.rs` grows rows for the comma list and its refusals; a panel table walks what the window writes for a set moved, nudged and deleted, for a handle turned with its partner, for a pair broken and for a vertex converted both ways, each read back as the points and handles it wrote; and a playtest sheet covers what neither can judge - whether a box catches what the hand drew around it and whether a curve bends the way the hand pulls it. No new file in `Fixtures/`: every gesture here writes points and handles whose drawing FX-MSK-001 to 019 and FX-SHP-001 to 017 already pin. Consequence if accepted: B-24i, several points chosen and moved together; B-24j, the bezier gestures and the pen's rebinding; `verification/B-24h_path_point_playtest.md` rewritten before it is played; documents 15 and 24 amended to match. **Written down at acceptance, from building it.** Whether a vertex is smooth is **read from its handles and not stored**: a point is smooth when both handles are out and point opposite ways along one line, which is exactly what makes the curve run through it without a corner. So no file changes, no schema changes, and a path drawn before any of this still says the truth about itself. **And the keyboard got the half it was owed.** Pulling a handle is a drag and a drag is a mouse, so **]** and **[** on a point that has been tabbed to lengthen and shorten its pair of handles along the line between its two neighbours - the direction a smooth point's handles take anyway - a tenth of the way to them a press, to nothing and back to a corner. Without those two keys, curving a path would have been the first thing in this window a person with no mouse could not do at all, and `verification/B-12c_keyboard_table.md` would have had to say so. **The ceiling of the evidence, stated plainly:** every gesture above is arithmetic in `app/ui/index.html`, and no test in this repository can run the page's own code. The panel table checks what the window's commands do with the points they are handed; whether the hand pulling a handle sees the curve it meant is the playtest sheets' to answer and nothing else's.

D-81 / The free transform box around a mask or a shape / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-23 by the owner ("proceed")**; proposed by the agent the same day, from the owner's choice of B-24k ("let's begin with 1 then 2"). D-80 named it as deferred. B-24k is built against it the same day. **It changes no file and no fixture.** Like D-80's gestures, the box writes every point and both of its handles through `mask.set_path` and `shape.set_path`, which exist, and whether a box is up is the window's own state, saved nowhere. **How it comes up, as in After Effects.** With the selection tool, a **double-click on a mask's or a shape's outline or on one of its points** puts a box around the whole of it. **Ctrl+T** puts the box around the points already chosen, or around the whole mask when fewer than two are chosen. Both keys are free today. The box is the smallest upright rectangle holding the points, not the handles. It has eight small squares, one at each corner and one at the middle of each side, and a cross-hair, the **anchor**, at its centre. **What the hand does with it.**
- **Inside the box, drag:** every point in it moves, as B-24i's drag does.
- **A corner or side square, drag:** scales the points against the **opposite** corner or side, which stays still. A side scales one way only. **Shift** on a corner keeps the box's proportions. **Ctrl** scales about the anchor instead of the opposite side. Dragging past the opposite side flips the points, as After Effects does.
- **Just outside the box, drag:** the pointer becomes a curved arrow and turns every point about the anchor. **Shift** holds the turn to steps of 45 degrees.
- **The anchor, drag:** moves the anchor alone, and nothing is drawn differently.
- **Enter, Escape, or a double-click outside the box:** takes the box away. Choosing another tool, layer or mask does too.

**What happens to the handles.** A handle is an offset from its point, so it is turned and scaled with its point but not moved with it. Stretching or turning a straight line keeps it straight, so a smooth point stays smooth (D-80 reads that from its handles) and a corner stays a corner, and the curve changes shape exactly as its points do. **Each drag is one entry in the history**, however many points it moved, and one Ctrl+Z takes back the whole of it. On a path with keys, the drag sets the path at the current frame, exactly as dragging a point does today, so the stopwatch works as it already does.

**What is left out, named rather than assumed.**
- **No skewing and no perspective.** After Effects' mask box scales and turns only, and so does this one.
- **One mask or shape at a time.** After Effects can put one box around several masks at once; D-80's choosing is one mask at a time, so that would need several masks chosen at once first.
- **No box around a whole layer.** A layer's Scale and Rotation already do that.
- **No keys of its own.** A mask can still be scaled or turned from the keyboard only point by point, with the arrow keys, as today. If the owner wants typed numbers for scale and turn, that is an amendment.
- **If every point is on one line**, the box has no width or no height, and scaling along that side changes nothing rather than dividing by nothing.

**Evidence if accepted.** Panel table rows for what the window sends when a box is scaled, turned and moved, read back as the points and handles it wrote. A playtest sheet covers what no table can judge: whether the box sits around the points, whether each square scales from the side it should, and whether a turn goes about the cross-hair. **The ceiling of the evidence, as for D-80:** the box's arithmetic is in `app/ui/index.html`, and no test here can run the page's own code. The playtest sheet is the only check on it. No new file in `Fixtures/`: what the box writes are points and handles whose drawing FX-MSK-001 to 019 and FX-SHP-001 to 017 already pin. Consequence if accepted: B-24k is built, and documents 15 and 24 are amended to match.

D-81a / The free transform box's limits / **ACCEPTED as direction on 2026-09-23 by the owner ("works; work on limits"), written by the agent as B-24l the same day**, the owner's answer to B-24k's playtest, whose sheet listed six limits. **It changes no file and no fixture**; the box still writes only through `mask.set_path` and `shape.set_path`. **Three limits are lifted.** *Several masks:* Shift and a double-click on another mask's outline adds that mask to the box, and every drag, scale and turn then moves every mask in it as one picture, one entry in the history; a plain double-click on another mask moves the box to that mask alone. *Keys:* with the box up, the arrow keys move what it holds a pixel a press, ten with Shift; **+** and **-** on the numeric keypad turn it a degree about the anchor, ten with Shift; with Alt they scale it one percent about the anchor, ten with Shift. Each press is one entry in the history. These are After Effects' own keypad keys for turning and scaling a layer, since After Effects' mask box has no keys of its own. *Undo:* the box remembers its turn and anchor for every shape it has held, so an Undo or Redo that puts a mask back also puts the box back as it stood around that shape, rather than leaving it turned. **Three are kept on purpose, because After Effects' mask box does not do them either:** skew and perspective, a box round a whole layer (the layer's own handles are that), and a box kept in the saved file. **The fourth is arithmetic:** points in one straight line give a box with no width, and there is nothing to scale across it. **Found while building it, and fixed:** B-24g's drag queue kept only the newest request of a whole drag, so a drag moving several layers, or now several masks, could drop the last step of all but one and leave them short of where the hand let go. It now keeps the newest request of each property. **Evidence.** `verification/B-24h_panel_table.md` grows three rows: one drag changing two masks' paths is one entry in the history, lands both, and one Undo puts both back. `verification/B-24l_box_limits_playtest.md` is the owner's sheet and, as for D-81, the only check on the box's arithmetic.

D-82 / Null layers: a layer that is never drawn, there to be a parent / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-23 by the owner ("proceed")**, proposed the same day by the agent as B-26a with its fixtures first, at the owner's word ("think we should add a null layer just in case?"). B-26b built the core against it and B-26c the window, the same day. **What is already there:** D-57 lets any layer be a parent, even one switched off, so a switched-off solid can stand in for a handle today. It is a stand-in and not a handle: switched on by mistake it draws a rectangle into the picture and the export, and its colour and size mean nothing. **The layer.** A new layer kind, `null`, as After Effects' null object is. It has no `asset_id`, no exposures, no source offset and no record of its own, no size, no colour. It has what a parent needs and what every layer has to be kept in order: name, switch, lock, in and out frames, transform, parent, depth, label and shy. Its transform and depth reach its children exactly as any parent's do by D-57 and D-58; its opacity is kept and can be keyed, and like any parent's it does not reach them. **It is never drawn.** Document 21's steps are skipped for it whole: whatever its switch, opacity or in and out frames say, a frame with a null in it is the frame without it, pixel for pixel, on the screen and in every export. **What it cannot carry**, because it has no picture to carry it on: a mask, an effect, a matte of its own, a blend mode other than normal, and it cannot be another layer's matte. A file that gives a null any of them, or an asset, exposures, a source offset, a solid record or shapes, is `PROJECT_SCHEMA_INVALID` (FX-NULL-020 to 029); no build writes any of them. The commands that would give it one refuse it in a sentence, as an audio layer's do under D-71. **A new null** is named `Null 1`, `Null 2` and so on, lasts the whole composition, sits above the chosen layer or else at the front, and stands at the composition's centre with its anchor at (50, 50), the middle of its outline. **In the window** it is drawn only as a guide, never into the frame: a thin 100 by 100 square in its own layer space, so it turns and scales with its transform, with the anchor's cross-hair, and it is dragged, turned and scaled on the picture as any layer is. Its bar on the timeline is its own, a thin grey strip, as each kind has its own look (B-20c), and its row says it is a null. **Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Y is not quite free today:** the window reads it as Ctrl+Alt+Y and makes an adjustment layer, so B-26c makes that key ask for Shift to be up. **Commands.** `layer.add_null`, one step of history, on **Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Y** as in After Effects and in the Layer menu as New Null. **Nothing to fetch.** A null has no media: it is never missing and a collected package has nothing of it to copy. **Not in this decision:** the camera parented to a null, After Effects' standard camera rig, because D-58 made the camera part of the composition rather than a layer, and nothing can be a camera's parent until that changes. **Evidence basis:** `Fixtures/null/`, FX-NULL-001 to 007 (frames) and 020 to 029 (refusals), from `tools/null_reference.py`, which carries the drawing through the parent chain with `tools/parent_reference.py`'s steps and moves by whole pixels only; document 25 shows them. Consequence if accepted: B-26b, the kind in the core and the file, its absence from every frame, the refusals and the command, with a table that walks FX-NULL-001 to 029; B-26c, the window: New Null, the outline on the picture, the grey strip, and a playtest sheet.
D-83 / The pick whip: drag from one property onto another to link them / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-23 by the owner ("proceed")**, proposed the same day by the agent as B-27a with its fixtures first, at the owner's word ("for null's and generally any other value across the layers, I want to be able to alt click, then click drag from stopwatch to other layers' or null value of say position, so that one is parent, etc connected like AE does. have a visual preview line as I drag from one point to another"), and the owner's "proceed" to writing it. B-27b built the core against it the same day. **What is already there:** D-57 makes a parent by choosing it from the Parent list, and D-59 links one value to another by typing an expression such as `thisComp.layer("null-1").transform.position` into the box that Alt-click on a stopwatch opens. Both work; neither can be done by pointing. **Two whips, as After Effects has them.** The **parent whip** is a small spiral on each layer's row in the layer list and beside the Parent list in the inspector. Dragged onto another layer's row it makes that layer the parent, exactly as choosing it from the Parent list does: the same `layer.set_parent`, the child keeps its place on the picture, one step of history, and a loop is refused with D-57's sentence. A sound is not a place to drop, as the Parent list offers none today (D-71), and the camera is not a layer (D-58). The **value whip** is a spiral on a property's row once that property has an expression, so Alt-click on its stopwatch first, as today, and the spiral appears beside the expression box. Dragged onto another property's row, in the layer list with that layer twirled open or in the camera's group, it replaces the whole expression with a link to that property: one new command, `property.link`, one step of history. **B-27b note:** in the core the link is `expr::link`, which writes the text or refuses in a sentence, and the step it makes is `property.set_expression`'s own, so Undo and the history name it as setting an expression. What can be dropped on is every property an expression can read under D-59: a layer's anchor point, position, scale, rotation, opacity and depth, on any layer including a null, and the camera's position, depth and zoom. **The text a drop writes** (FX-WHIP-001 to 013). A layer is named by its id, as D-59 names it, so renaming the layer does not break the link: `thisComp.layer("null-1").transform.position`, with After Effects' own words, so the anchor is `anchorPoint`. The camera is `thisComp.activeCamera.position`. Two numbers onto one takes the first, x: `...position[0]`. One number onto two uses it for both: `temp = ...rotation;` then `[temp, temp]` on the next line. Anything else is written as it is. The text is ordinary D-59 text: it can be edited, switched off or cleared afterwards like any expression, and it saves and reopens as any does. **What a drop does not check.** A link that closes a loop is written, and D-59's rule then applies: each property in the loop falls back to its own keys and shows EXPRESSION_CYCLE beside its box (FX-WHIP-013), as After Effects does. Dropping a property on itself writes nothing (FX-WHIP-020). **While dragging.** A thin line runs from the spiral to the pointer; a row that can take the drop lights up as the pointer crosses it, and a label beside the pointer names what it would link to, such as "Null 1 › Position" or "Camera › Zoom"; a row that cannot take it stays dark and the label says why, such as "a sound cannot be a parent". Letting go on a lit row does the one step. Letting go anywhere else, or pressing Escape, draws nothing and changes nothing. **Not in this decision:** effect settings as places to drop, because D-68 gives them keys and no expression, so nothing could read them; dropping onto a layer's outline on the picture, which After Effects does not do either; a spiral on a property with no expression, which After Effects shows only in its Parent & Link column; and twirling a closed layer open by hovering over it mid-drag, so a layer's properties are twirled open before the drag starts. **Checks.** B-27b adds `property.link` in the core and a table that walks FX-WHIP-001 to 020 against `Fixtures/pickwhip/expected_pickwhip.json`: the text written, then each linked value against the expected one on frames 0, 12, 24, 36 and 48. B-27c adds the spirals, the line, the lit row and the label to the window, with a table that the parent whip sends what the Parent list sends, and a playtest sheet for what only a person can judge: that the line follows the hand and the right row lights. **B-27c note:** the spiral is an @ sign in blue. The value whip sits on the Expression row under a property in the layer list, between its switch and its name, and after the switch in the inspector, the camera's rows included. A drop on a row sends `property.link` with the dragged property as `layer`/`target` and `prop` and the row's as `from_layer`/`from_target` and `from_prop`. The keyboard table counts `property.link` as a mouse gesture, like `effect.move`: what it writes can be typed into the expression box, and the parent whip's result is the Parent list's.

D-84 / Import a cut from its XDTS timesheet / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-24 by the owner ("cool, proceed")**, amended the same day by the owner's answer to its own check (below), and proposed on 2026-09-23 by the agent as B-28a, with its fixtures first, at the owner's word ("let's proceed with the first build, I want to learn this later ... I might pull from CSP, OpenToonz, Toon Boom, or paper scanned by a studio; no real files unfortunately. let's say through import no need for internet functionality; hmmm, let's do layer bars for now"), taking up document 15's reuse entry R-01. **Why now, without the evidence AR-08 asks for.** Document 31's AR-08 asks for real timesheets before this is built, and there are none. The owner chose it anyway, as preparation for learning how a timesheet drives a compositor, so every sheet in the fixtures is synthetic, written from CELSYS's public specification ("XDTS file format", 2018/11/29) and from no one's reader. **What a person does.** Import Cut asks for a folder: the cut's folder, holding one `.xdts` file and the drawings for its columns. The folder is the person's choice, so reading inside it keeps document 07's rule that only chosen places are searched; nothing outside it, and nothing deeper than one folder down, is read. What arrives is a new composition, opened, with one layer per drawing column, as one step of history that Undo takes back whole. **The sheet, as read.** The first line must be `exchangeDigitalTimeSheet Save Data`, with a byte-order mark and Windows line endings allowed, and the rest JSON; otherwise nothing is imported. The first timetable is read. Its `duration` is the composition's length. The file says no frame rate, so the composition is 24 frames a second, anime's usual rate, and the status line says so; it can be changed afterwards as any composition's can. The composition is named after the timetable, or after the file when the timetable has no name, and is the size most of its drawings share. Each track of the cell field (`fieldId` 0) is a column, named from `timeTableHeaders`. Columns stack by track number, 0 at the bottom as the specification says, whatever order the file lists them in. Frames count from 0. **A cell.** The specification writes a column only where something changes, so an entry holds until the next one, and the last to the end of the sheet. A whole number is a drawing number. SYMBOL_NULL_CELL is a blank cell, the cross on a paper sheet: nothing is shown from there to the next entry. SYMBOL_HYPHEN continues what was there. The two tick marks, SYMBOL_TICK_1 (inbetween) and SYMBOL_TICK_2 (reverse sheet), change nothing shown and are reported with their frames. The same drawing written twice in a row is one exposure. Anything else, such as `3a`, a full-width digit or no value at all, is reported with its frame and value, and the column is blank from there to its next entry, so the gap shows rather than being covered. An entry past the end of the sheet, or a second entry on one frame, is left out and reported; the first on a frame is kept. An entry before frame 0 is carried in, by the check below: the last one stands on frame 0 unless frame 0 has its own entry, and is reported as TIMESHEET_ENTRY_CARRIED_IN; any others before frame 0 are left out and reported. **This reading of holds is what the specification implies without saying it in words.** B-28b checks it against OpenToonz's BSD-3 reader before building on it, and if the two differ this decision comes back to the owner before any code. **The check, on 2026-09-24,** read `toonz/sources/toonz/xdtsio.cpp` at OpenToonz commit 232cdf7d80 (2026-09-16). It agrees on holds, the last entry to the end, blank cells, the hyphen, the tick marks and the order of the columns. It differed in one way that changes what is shown: since commit 23910493a1 (2020) it carries in an entry written before frame 0, which its comment says Clip Studio Paint may export although the specification does not allow it, and this decision had left such an entry out. The owner chose to carry it in ("Carry it in"), and FX-XDTS-028 was added before any code. Two smaller differences stay as written: OpenToonz reads `3a` as a drawing with a letter, which this program's drawings cannot have, so it stays a reported blank; and two entries on one frame shift OpenToonz's later frames by one, where this decision keeps the first and reports the second. **Drawings.** A column's drawings are the drawing files in a folder beside the sheet with the column's name, compared without regard to case; failing that, loose files beside the sheet named for the column and then `_`, `-`, `.` or a space and a number, such as `A_0001.png`. A folder wins over loose files. Numbers are read as `media.import` reads them, the last run of digits in the name, and every rule it already has for gaps, duplicates and sizes applies unchanged. Each column becomes one image sequence and one layer from frame 0 to the end, holding the sheet's exposures. **Nothing is dropped quietly (document 28).** A drawing the sheet calls for that is not there keeps its timing, so those frames say MEDIA_SEQUENCE_GAP when drawn, and the import names it. Also named: drawings present and never shown; folders and drawings beside the sheet that match no column, such as a background; a column with no drawings, no name or only blank cells; a dialogue or camerawork column; a second timetable; and a version other than 5. The sixteen IDs are listed in document 25 and go into document 28 at B-28b. **Where it came from.** Each layer made records the sheet's file, the column's name and its track number, saved with the layer as `timesheet` only when set, as `parent` is. Nothing reads it in this build. It is there so a later build can offer to update a layer's timing when its sheet changes without asking which column was which. **Not in this decision:** a timesheet view in the window, since the layer bars and exposures already show the timing; writing XDTS back out; reading dialogue or camerawork as markers; the older TDTS format and CSP's CSV; paper sheets, which cannot be read and would first have to be typed into a program that saves XDTS; updating an imported cut from a changed sheet; and any network use. Clip Studio Paint and OpenToonz save XDTS, at least in recent versions; whether Toon Boom Harmony does was not confirmed. **Checks.** FX-XDTS-001 to 040 in document 25, from `tools/xdts_reference.py`, which writes each cut into `Fixtures/xdts/` and what it must become into `Fixtures/xdts/expected_xdts.json`. B-28b reads every cut in the core and compares the composition, each layer's name, order, exposures, drawings and record, and the notes by ID and facts, in any order. B-28c adds Import Cut to the window, with a table and a playtest sheet on FX-XDTS-040, a two-second sample cut made to be played and learned from. A plain-language introduction to timesheets is `research/2026-09-23_timesheet_primer.md`.

D-84a / The Sheet view / **ACCEPTED as direction on 2026-09-24 by the owner ("approved; proceed")**, written by the agent as B-28d the same day, the owner's answer to the agent's recommendation after they asked for "a way to maybe toggle it's view, maybe a new workspace type". **It changes no file and no fixture, and it edits nothing**: it is a third way of looking at the composition on screen. **Not a workspace:** the timeline panel gains a third tab, Sheet, beside Timeline and Graph, and the rest of the window stays as it is. **The grid:** frames run down the page, one row a frame, with the frame number on the left and a heavier line under the last frame of every second, at the composition's rate. There is a column for each layer that shows an image sequence, the bottom of the stack on the left and the top on the right, as a paper timesheet and document 25's FX-XDTS-040 table are laid out; a layer of any other kind has no column. **A cell** is what a paper sheet has written in it: the drawing's number on the frame it is first exposed, a line down the cells that hold it, a cross (x) on the frame a blank run starts and nothing while it lasts, and shading outside the layer's in and out. A drawing exposed again straight after itself is a hold, as on paper. **Every cell comes from the core's own answer** to which drawing a layer shows on a frame (`ExposureMap::drawing_at` after `LayerTiming::local_frame`, the two the picture is drawn from), worked out in the window's Rust side and asked for by the page as `/sheet` on the frame scheme, as `/curve` is for the graph, so the sheet cannot disagree with the picture and a table can check it. **The current frame's row is highlighted**, and clicking a row puts the playhead there. Any image-sequence layer has a column, whether it came from a timesheet or not. **Not in this step:** typing into the sheet, dialogue and camera columns, and printing it; each is its own decision if the owner asks.

D-85 / Workspaces / **ACCEPTED as direction on 2026-09-24 by the owner**, who chose "Slot workspaces (Recommended)" and "Workspaces first (Recommended)" from the agent's choices after asking "should we start building modular sections that we can move around already like AE does? and then have a reset workspace/build workspace now?"; written by the agent as B-29 the same day. **It changes no project file and no fixture:** a workspace is how this window is laid out. It is kept in the browser's storage beside the panel sizes, as W-13 keeps them, and a project opened on another machine lays out however that machine last had it. **Places:** the window keeps document 24's four places, left, centre, right and bottom, and the borders between them. **Panels:** five of them: Project, Composition, Effect controls, Timeline (still with its Timeline and Graph tabs) and Sheet. The Sheet leaves the timeline panel and becomes a panel of its own. That amends D-84a's "not a workspace", and it is what lets the sheet stand as a tall column beside the picture, as a paper sheet does. **A place holds any number of panels, one in front;** with more than one, a row of their names above them brings one forward. **Moving a panel:** drag its name or its title bar onto another place, or right-click either for "Move to the left, centre, right or bottom"; it arrives in front. A side place or the bottom left with no panel folds away with its border, and the menu brings a panel back to it. **The bottom keeps its height** whichever panel is in front (a third of the window until its border is pulled), so bringing the Sheet forward cannot take room from the viewer. That is what the owner's screenshot of the Sheet tab showed. **The Workspace list** in the command strip has two built-in workspaces and any the person saves. Standard is document 24's G1 default: Project left, Composition centre, Effect controls right, and Timeline bottom with the Sheet behind it. Timing puts the Sheet in front on the left with Project behind it and the left column wider, and is otherwise as Standard. **Save workspace...** keeps the current arrangement and sizes under a name. A built-in name is refused, so Standard can always be had back. **Reset workspace** puts the current one back as it was built or saved, and replaces Preferences' "Put the panel sizes back". The ` key fills the window with the place under the pointer. The window opens in Standard until the person chooses another, so document 24's W-01 contract holds. **Not in this step:** floating windows, splitting a place in two, deleting a saved workspace, a workspace keeping unsaved changes when another is chosen, and moving a panel from the keyboard.

D-84b / Writing into the Sheet / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-24 by the owner ("proceed")**, proposed by the agent the same day as the first of the three the owner asked for after D-84a ("let's do all three of these in order"), with FX-SHEET-001 to 016 in document 25; built as B-28e the same day. **It changes no file format and adds no core command:** writing a cell is one `SetExposureSpans`, the command the exposure list already sends, so it is one entry in the history and Undo puts the column back. The window's Rust side works out the new exposures from the old, as it works out the grid, and the page asks for it as `exposure.write?layer=...&frame=...&mark=...`. **A cell means what it means on paper:** a number or a cross written on a frame lasts until the next thing written below it in the column, and replaces whatever was shown on those frames. Written where a line runs, a number starts that drawing there; written on a number, it replaces it; written in a blank, it starts the drawing there and the blank ends. A cross does the same with nothing. **Erasing** a number or a cross lets what is written above it run on through the frames it covered. That lengthens the exposure above rather than adding a second one, and with nothing above, those frames go blank. A cell with nothing written in it (a line, or the empty cells after a cross) has nothing to erase, and the window says so. Writing the drawing a frame already shows changes nothing and adds nothing to the history. **The rest of the column is left as it was**, including two exposures of one drawing side by side, which the sheet shows as one hold (FX-SHEET-012). A blank that runs to the end of the layer runs to its out point, so a number written in it lasts to there. **In the window:** click a cell to choose it, and the playhead goes to its frame as a click on a row does now. Type digits and press Enter to write a number, press x to write a cross, and Delete or Backspace to erase. After writing, the chosen cell moves down a row, as a pencil moves down the sheet. The arrow keys move the chosen cell, and Escape drops what is being typed. A shaded cell, outside the layer, cannot be chosen. A number with no drawing in the layer's sequence is written anyway, and the answer says so, as the exposure list's does. **Not in this step:** writing several frames or columns at once (a range, or filling on twos), copying and pasting cells, dragging a mark, and writing outside a layer's in and out.

D-84c / Dialogue and camera columns / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-24 by the owner ("proceed")**, proposed by the agent the same day as the second of the three the owner asked for after D-84a ("let's do all three of these in order"), with FX-XDTS-019 and amended expectations for FX-XDTS-014, 034 and 040 in document 25; built as B-28f. **It changes the project file and three fixtures' expected notes**, which is why it waited for the owner's word before any code. **What a person sees.** Importing a cut whose sheet has a dialogue or camera column keeps them, and the Sheet shows them as a paper timesheet does: dialogue columns left of the drawing columns, camera columns right of them. A line of dialogue or a camera instruction is written on the frame it starts, with a line down the frames it lasts, and nothing where there is none. FX-XDTS-040, the sample cut, shows "MIKA Over here!" from frame 0 to 15 and "FOLLOW" from frame 20 to 47. Clicking a text cell moves the playhead as a click on its row does. **The sheet, as read.** Field 3 of the XDTS file is dialogue and field 5 is camerawork; each of their tracks becomes a text column. Its name is the sheet's header for that field and track, or "Dialogue" or "Camera" when the header gives none. An entry is the list of strings written on a frame, kept as written (a speaker and a line are two strings), and lasts from that frame through the SYMBOL_HYPHEN written on each frame straight after it, as the specification writes a held line; so an entry with no hyphen after it lasts one frame. SYMBOL_NULL_CELL is nothing. A hyphen with nothing running above it, anything other than strings, an entry outside the sheet and a second entry on one frame are left out and reported as TIMESHEET_ENTRY_IGNORED, with the column, frames and reason, as for the drawing columns. Unlike a drawing, an entry before frame 0 is not carried in. Any other field is still reported as TIMESHEET_FIELD_NOT_READ. A sheet refused for having no drawing columns is refused as before, and its text is not reported. **Where it is kept.** The composition gains `sheet_text`, a list of text columns, each `kind` ("dialogue" or "camera"), `name`, `track` and `entries`, each entry `start_frame`, `end_frame_exclusive` and `text`, a list of strings. It is saved only when there are some, as `markers` is, so every project saved before this reads and saves unchanged. It comes in with the import, so the one Undo that takes back the import takes it too. A column of another `kind`, which a later version might write, is kept, saved back and shown on the right; a malformed `sheet_text` refuses the file with the place it is wrong, as a malformed marker does (document 28). **The window.** `/sheet` answers with the text columns beside the drawing columns, each cell the entry's text on its first frame, a line after it, or nothing, so a table can check the Sheet against document 25. **Checks.** `tools/xdts_reference.py`, the second reader, reads the two fields the same way and writes the new expectations into `Fixtures/xdts/expected_xdts.json` before any code; B-28b's test then compares each cut's text columns as it compares layers, and B-28f adds a table of the Sheet's text cells for FX-XDTS-040 and a playtest sheet. The B-28c table's count for the sample cut goes from four notes to two. **Not in this step:** typing or changing text in the Sheet, adding a text column by hand, text on anything but an imported cut, showing dialogue in the viewer or on the timeline, and writing XDTS back out.

D-84d / Printing the Sheet / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-24 by the owner ("proceed")**, proposed by the agent the same day as the third of the three the owner asked for after D-84a ("let's do all three of these in order"; the owner chose "Print / PDF" over a file export), with FX-PRINT-001 to 004 in document 25; built as B-28g. It changes nothing in the project file or the fixtures already accepted. **What a person sees.** The Sheet's title bar gains **Print...**, and Ctrl+P does the same anywhere in the window (without it, Ctrl+P prints the window itself, which is of no use). It opens the system's print dialog on the composition on screen laid out as a paper timesheet, black on white, where the printer can be a real one or Microsoft Print to PDF. **The paper.** A page holds six seconds, as a Japanese A4 timesheet does: two halves side by side, three seconds each, the left half first. At 24 frames a second that is 144 frames a page and 72 a half. A cut takes as many pages as it needs, at least one. The frames past the cut's end are printed as empty rows, and a heavy line goes under its last frame.
