Each page has a header: the cut's name, "Sheet n of m", its length as seconds + frames (48 frames at 24 is "2 + 0", 300 is "12 + 12") and its frame rate. Each half has the same columns as the Sheet on screen, in the same order, and each cell holds what that cell shows on screen: a number, a hold line, a cross, the words of a dialogue or camera entry, or grey outside a layer. A heavier line marks the end of each second, as on screen. **How it is made.** The window writes the whole printable page itself, from the same cells as `/sheet`, and answers it at `/sheet/print`; the page puts it in a hidden frame and asks the system to print that frame. (Changed at B-28g's first playtest, the same day: the window's content security policy refused the frame's styles and the owner's PDF came out a bare table, so the pages go into the window's own page, hidden, and a style in that page, between its `sheet paper` marks, shows only them when printing; the printable page the window writes copies that style, so the interface stays one file. The page has no margins of its own, so the print dialog prints no date or address on it.) So what prints cannot differ from the Sheet, and a table can check the pages without a printer. A composition with no drawing layers has nothing to print: Print... is not offered, and Ctrl+P says so in the status line. **Checks.** FX-PRINT-001 to 004 in document 25 give each case's pages, halves, header and end line; B-28g's table reads them from document 25 and checks the page the window writes, and checks that every printed cell matches the Sheet's. It also writes the sample cut's printable page into `verification/` to open in any browser. A playtest sheet has the owner print the sample cut to PDF and look at it. **Not in this step:** choosing the page size or seconds per page in the window (the dialog's own paper and orientation settings apply), a title block with the production's name, scene and animator, printing more than the composition on screen, and writing XDTS back out.

D-84e / The paper sheet, laid out as a studio's / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-24 by the owner ("proceed")**, proposed by the agent the same day as the first of three written after B-28g's second look ("looks great! let's do 1 through 7", of the seven the agent listed after the owner asked what else official sheets have), covering items 1, 4, 5, 6 and 7, with FX-PRINT-005 to 008 and amended expectations for FX-PRINT-001 to 003 in document 25; to be built as B-28h. **It changes three fixtures' expected frame numbers and columns, and nothing in the project file.** **Frames counted from 1.** On paper the cut's first frame is row 1, as on a studio's sheet: row n is the cut's nth frame. The sample cut's rows with drawings are 1 to 48, its end line is under 48, and at 24 frames a second the heavy line of each second is under 24, 48, 72 and so on. Only the paper counts from 1. The Sheet on screen keeps the timeline's numbers, which the playhead and every other panel use, so frame 47 on screen is row 48 on paper; counting from 1 in the whole window would be a separate decision. **Second numbers.** A narrow column, headed sec, at the left of each half holds the second's number on the row that ends it: 1 beside row 24, 2 beside 48, and on through the pages, so page 2 at 6 seconds a page starts at 7. Rows past the cut's end keep theirs, as a printed form does. **The Action column.** Each half has an Action column left of the dialogue, as a studio's sheet does, printed empty to write in by hand; D-84g puts what is typed there. **Six cel columns.** Each half has at least six drawing columns, as a paper sheet's A to F. When the composition has fewer drawing layers, the rest are printed empty, with empty headings, to be written in by hand; when it has more, all are printed, narrower. **Seconds a page.** Print... and Ctrl+P now open a small window, Print the Sheet, before the system's print dialog. It offers 6 seconds a page, two halves of three, as now, or 3 seconds a page, one column of three seconds with taller rows. At 24 frames a second, 3 seconds is 72 frames a page. **Colour.** The same small window offers the sheet in black, as now, or in red, as studios' printed forms are. In red, what the form prints is red: its rules, headings, frame and second numbers, and the title block's labels. What is written on it stays black: the numbers, lines, crosses and words in the cells, and the title block's entries. The two choices are remembered in the window for the next print, and are not saved in the project. `/sheet/print` takes them as `seconds` (6 or 3) and `colour` (black or red); anything else writes no pages and says what it takes. **The Sheet on screen is unchanged.** **Checks.** FX-PRINT-001 to 003 are amended for frames from 1, the second numbers, the Action column and six cel columns; FX-PRINT-005 to 008 add 3 seconds a page, red, and a refused choice. B-28g's table reads them as before, and a playtest sheet has the owner print the sample cut both ways and in red. **Not in this step:** counting from 1 on screen, other page sizes (the dialog's paper setting applies), and seconds a page other than 3 and 6.

D-84f / The title block / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-24 by the owner ("proceed")**, proposed by the agent the same day as the second of three written after B-28g's second look ("looks great! let's do 1 through 7", of the seven the agent listed after the owner asked what else official sheets have), item 2, with FX-PRINT-009 and 010 and an amended header for FX-PRINT-001 in document 25; to be built as B-28i after B-28h. **It changes the project file.** **What a person sees.** Composition Settings (Ctrl+K) gains four boxes under a heading, Sheet: Episode, Scene, Cut and Animator. What is written in them prints in the title block, in boxes labelled EPISODE, SCENE, CUT and ANIMATOR; an empty one prints empty, to fill in by hand. The composition's name keeps its box, now labelled NAME (it was CUT). The title block is two rows: NAME, EPISODE, SCENE, CUT and ANIMATOR above, and TIME, RATE, SHEET and MEMO below. Changing them is part of Composition Settings' one step, so one Undo takes them back with the rest. **Where they are kept.** The composition gains `sheet_details`, an object of `episode`, `scene`, `cut` and `animator`, each a string. It is saved only when one of them is not empty, as `markers` is, so every project saved before this reads and saves unchanged. A key in it that this version does not know is kept and saved back; one of the four that is not a string refuses the file with the place it is wrong (document 28). `SET_COMPOSITION_SETTINGS` carries them. **Checks.** FX-PRINT-009 prints the sample cut with all four written, and FX-PRINT-010 saves and opens it again; B-28g's table checks the header's boxes, and a playtest sheet has the owner fill them in and print. **Not in this step:** reading the scene and cut from an XDTS file's header (the sample cuts' headers all say scene 1, cut 1, whatever their names), and other boxes, such as the in-betweener or the production.

D-84g / The Action column and key drawings / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-24 by the owner ("proceed")**, proposed by the agent the same day as the third of three written after B-28g's second look ("looks great! let's do 1 through 7", of the seven the agent listed after the owner asked what else official sheets have), item 3, with FX-SHEET-017 to 024, FX-PRINT-011 and an amended Sheet for FX-XDTS-040 in document 25; to be built as B-28j after B-28i. **It changes the project file and adds two core commands.** **The Action column.** The Sheet gains an Action column at its left, left of the dialogue, as on paper. Every composition with drawing layers has one, empty until something is written in it. Click an Action cell and type: Enter writes the words on that frame and moves the chosen cell down a row, Escape drops them, and Delete erases what is written on that frame. A note is on its one frame only, with no line after it. Writing on a frame that has a note replaces it, and writing nothing, or only spaces, is refused. Printed, the Action column holds the notes (D-84e prints it). It is kept as a D-84c text column of kind `action`, named Action, track 0, each note an entry one frame long, saved only when there are some, so D-84c's rules for `sheet_text` apply unchanged. The new core command `SET_SHEET_TEXT` replaces a composition's text columns as one, the whole list being the unit as it is for `SET_MARKERS`, so each note written or erased is one entry in the history. **Key drawings.** Choose a drawing cell showing a number and press K: that drawing is marked as a key of its layer, and every cell where the layer's number for it is written is circled, on screen and on paper. K on a cell of a key drawing unmarks it. A cell showing a line, a cross or nothing cannot be marked, and the window says so. While a cell is chosen, K marks rather than going to the next keyframe. Kept on the layer as `key_drawings`, the list of drawing numbers, in order, saved only when there are some; a drawing the sequence does not have is kept. The new core command `SET_KEY_DRAWINGS` replaces a layer's list, one entry in the history. `/sheet` answers each drawing column's keys. **Checks.** FX-SHEET-017 to 024 write and erase notes, mark and unmark keys, and save and open them again; FX-PRINT-011 prints them. B-28e's and B-28g's tables read them as before, and a playtest sheet has the owner write a note, circle a key and print. **Not in this step:** notes that last several frames, typing in the dialogue and camera columns, several Action columns, marking keys on anything but a drawing layer, and reading or writing keys in XDTS files.

D-86 / Line smoothing / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-25 by the owner ("proceed with B")**, proposed by the agent the same day after the owner chose document 15's reuse entry R-02 ("ok, let's do line smoothing, would this constitute as being worthy of being in the effects panel like R-03 and R-04?"), with three comparison pictures in `verification/B-30a proposal/`: A, OpenToonz's method as it is, and B, the same with corners kept sharp. The owner chose B. FX-SMOOTH-001 to 022 in document 25 are its fixtures; to be built as B-30b and B-30c. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** A drawing made without antialiasing, as cel lines are, has stair steps where two flat colours meet. Line smoothing finds each step and puts back the straight slope it stands for, mixing the two colours along it, and leaves flat colour and straight edges alone. It is the fourth effect, beside exposure, tint and blur: `core.line_smooth`, named Line Smoothing in the Effects panel. **Settings:** `softness`, 0 to 100, starting at 50, how long the slope is: 0 changes nothing; and `threshold`, 0 to 255, starting at 10, how different two colours may be and still count as one, so that a scan's slight noise is not taken for an edge. Both can be keyed (D-68); a keyed value is held inside its range at each frame. **Where the method comes from.** It is Reshetov's morphological antialiasing as OpenToonz does it in `toonz/sources/common/trop/tantialias.cpp`, commit 6571328019e3a6a99c13f408ee6f4755c9cddf73 (2022-04-07, the last to touch that file; OpenToonz master was 16661c84 on 2026-09-25), under OpenToonz's BSD 3-Clause licence, copyright DWANGO Co., Ltd. and the respective contributors, 2016 to 2026. As document 10 asks, the origin and licence are recorded before any code: the licence text is kept whole in `docs/third_party/OpenToonz-LICENSE.txt`, the notice heads both the reference tool `tools/smooth_reference.py` and the build's port, and B-30b makes the packaged build carry the licence file. It is the same method OLM's page says OLM Smoother uses. **Three changes from OpenToonz,** each pinned by a fixture. First, two colours are the same when no channel differs by more than threshold/255, so a difference exactly at the threshold counts as the same (OpenToonz's is strictly less than). Second, colours are compared and mixed as a drawing program stores them: each pixel's straight colour through the sRGB curve, premultiplied by its alpha. That keeps a black line's weight as it was drawn, where mixing in linear light would thin it, and a line on nothing mixes only with nothing, so it gets no grey or white fringe (FX-SMOOTH-007 to 009). A pixel the method does not mix keeps its exact value. Third, the corner guard, the owner's choice B: the end of a run of 4 pixels or more whose crossing edge also runs 4 pixels or more is a corner, and is left sharp. OpenToonz takes such a corner for a step and shades half of each side of a box (FX-SMOOTH-005). **Where it runs.** On the drawing's own pixels, before the layer is moved, scaled or turned, as every effect on a drawing does (ADR-017), so a held drawing is smoothed the same on every frame it is held (FX-SMOOTH-013). It never reaches outside the drawing. **Order.** Added from the Effects panel, it goes to the top of the layer's stack, since smoothing a line after a blur or tint would find no steps to smooth; it can be moved as any effect can. **Out of range.** A command with a softness outside 0 to 100 or a threshold outside 0 to 255 is refused with a sentence. A file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 and FX-FXK-009 do (FX-SMOOTH-020 to 022). **Known limits:** a very shallow line, whose steps are long, becomes a long soft fade along each step; and a corner shorter than 4 pixels on either side is still rounded (FX-SMOOTH-006). **Checks.** B-30b adds the effect to the core and a table that renders every FX-SMOOTH case and compares it with `Fixtures/smooth/expected_smooth.json`. B-30c adds it to the Effects panel with its two settings, a panel table, and a playtest sheet on a real drawing. **Not in this decision:** choosing which line colours are smoothed, as OLM Smoother can; making lines thicker or thinner; and `loilo-inc/smooth`'s method, which stays R-02's second opinion.

D-87 / Selective colour blur / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-25 by the owner ("accept")**, proposed by the agent the same day after the owner took up document 15's reuse entry R-03, the cel colour operations, and chose selective colour blur as its first operation, with three pictures in `verification/B-31a proposal/`. FX-SELBLUR-001 to 024 in document 25 are its fixtures; to be built as B-31b and B-31c. **It adds one effect, changes where Line Smoothing is put when it is added (D-86), and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It softens the edge where two chosen cel colours meet, such as skin and its shadow, which a painter draws with no line between, and leaves every colour that is not chosen, lines above all, exactly as drawn: a chosen colour mixes only with chosen colours, and the mixing stops at the first pixel that is not chosen. It is the fifth effect, beside exposure, tint, blur and line smoothing: `core.selective_color_blur`, named Selective Colour Blur in the Effects panel. **Settings:** `blur`, 0 to 200 pixels, starting at 12, how far the softening reaches; it can be keyed (D-68), and its value at each frame is held inside its range and rounded to a whole pixel, a half rounding up. `colors`, the chosen colours, up to eight, each written `"#rrggbb"`, read in either case and written in small letters; it cannot be keyed, and it starts empty, which changes nothing, so an effect just added is valid. **Where the method comes from.** F's Plugins SelectiveColorBlur, `SelectiveColorBlur/SelectiveColorBlurSub.cpp` in bryful/F-s-PluginsProjects, commit db6dad3959522cfcd593dfe12a9fa4ad022d31e3 (2026-05-04), under the MIT licence, copyright 2019 bryful. The OpenFX port in cr-market/FsPluginsOFX (commit 49721c2dca455cd98c97e344a92802026f2989cd, MIT) was read and is not used; the original is the authority. As document 10 asks, the origin and licence are recorded before any code: the licence text is kept whole in `docs/third_party/F-s-PluginsProjects-LICENSE.txt`, the notice heads both the reference tool `tools/selblur_reference.py` and the build's port, and B-31b makes the packaged build carry the licence file. **What is kept from the original:** a pixel is chosen when its 8-bit colour equals a chosen colour exactly (FX-SELBLUR-008); colours are mixed as a drawing program stores them, the straight colour through the sRGB curve, not in linear light, so a mix is the one a painter would make; each chosen pixel becomes a Gaussian-weighted average of itself and the chosen pixels on either side, out to the blur, each side stopping at the first pixel that is not chosen or at the edge of the drawing, the weights made to sum to one; the weights are always the full blur's; and the passes are the original's five: across and down at the full blur, then across, down and across at a quarter, a sixteenth and a sixty-fourth of it, a pass whose reach comes to nothing left out, each reading the one before. **Two changes,** each pinned by a fixture. First, the original makes every chosen pixel fully opaque; D-87 keeps each pixel's own covering, so a half-covering chosen pixel stays half covering (FX-SELBLUR-007), and a pixel that does not show at all is never chosen, whatever its colour (FX-SELBLUR-006). Second, the original's 8-bit path rounds to whole steps after every pass; D-87 keeps the exact result, as the original's floating-point path does. **Where it runs.** On the drawing's own pixels, before the layer is moved, scaled or turned, as every effect on a drawing does (ADR-017), so a held drawing is softened the same on every frame it is held (FX-SELBLUR-010). It never reaches outside the drawing, and a pixel that is not chosen keeps its exact value. **Order.** Added from the Effects panel, it goes to the top of the layer's stack, since after a tint or a blur the colours no longer match exactly. D-86 is amended: Line Smoothing, added, now goes to the top but below any Selective Colour Blur already at the top, since smoothing first would mix new colours into the edges that the selective blur needs flat. Either can be moved as any effect can. **Out of range.** A command with a blur outside 0 to 200, more than eight colours, or a colour not written `#` and six hexadecimal digits is refused with a sentence. A file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 and FX-FXK-009 do (FX-SELBLUR-020 to 024). A `colors` that is missing or is not a list of strings is a fault in the file's shape, as a missing or mistyped setting of any effect is. **Known limits:** a colour one 8-bit step away from a chosen one is not chosen (FX-SELBLUR-008), so a drawing that was antialiased, scanned or saved lossy has few exact colours and gains little; and a line between two chosen colours stops the softening completely, which is the point, but a gap in the line lets it through. **Checks.** B-31b adds the effect to the core and a table that renders every FX-SELBLUR case and compares it with `Fixtures/selblur/expected_selblur.json`. B-31c adds it to the Effects panel with its Blur box and up to eight colour boxes, a panel table, and a playtest sheet on a real drawing. **Not in this decision:** R-03's other operations, main-line repaint and select colour; a tolerance for near colours; and choosing a colour by clicking the picture.

D-88 / Selective colour blur's tolerance / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-25 by the owner** ("let's add in a tolerance bar/slider, default as off", then "let's do tolerance"), after the owner tried D-87 on two drawings of their own, a painted background with 221,943 colours and a flat drawing whose chosen colours were its lines. FX-SELBLUR-025 to 033 in document 25 are its fixtures; to be built as B-32b and B-32c. **It adds one setting to D-87's effect and changes no existing fixture.** **The setting:** `tolerance`, 0 to 255, starting at 0, which is D-87 exactly: a pixel is chosen when it shows and each of its red, green and blue, in 8-bit steps, is within the tolerance of the same chosen colour's. At 0 that is an exact match (FX-SELBLUR-008); at 1 a colour one step off counts (FX-SELBLUR-027); at 255 every colour that shows counts (FX-SELBLUR-029). It can be keyed (D-68) and is held inside its range at each frame. **It is not rounded:** a colour differs by whole steps, so 0.5 takes in nothing that 0 does not (FX-SELBLUR-028), and a keyed tolerance takes in a colour at the frame it reaches the step. **In a file** it is written only when it is not 0 or is keyed, so a project saved before D-88 opens at 0 and saves exactly as it was. A command or file outside 0 to 255 is refused or bypassed as blur is (FX-SELBLUR-032, 033). **Everything else is D-87's:** the softening still stops at the first pixel that is not chosen, so a tolerance large enough to take in the lines softens them too (FX-SELBLUR-030). A draft preview does not scale it, since it is a distance in colour, not in pixels. **Checks.** B-32b adds it to the core and the B-31b table, which renders every FX-SELBLUR case; B-32c adds a Tolerance box under Blur on the card and a playtest sheet.

D-89 / Glow / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-25 by the owner ("proceed")**; proposed the same day by the agent after the owner took up document 15's reuse entry R-04, the blur and glow family, and chose glow first ("perfect! let's proceed"), with glow lit by "Both, as a switch", its light in "Its own colours, or a tint", and "I am essentially thinking of how AE does glow since it's what I am used to". Five pictures in `verification/B-33a proposal/`. FX-GLOW-001 to 033 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-33b and B-33c. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It makes the bright parts of a picture, or the colours chosen for it, shine: a blurred copy of them is laid on top, brightening them and spreading past the drawing's edge into the space around it, which it fills with light. It is the sixth effect: `core.glow`, named Glow in the Effects panel. **Settings, named as After Effects names them, with its defaults:** `based_on`, Glow Based On, either Bright parts (`"bright"`, the default) or Chosen colours (`"colors"`); `threshold`, Glow Threshold, 0 to 100 per cent, starting at 60, used with Bright parts: a pixel glows when its brightest channel, in 8-bit steps as a drawing program stores it, is at least that share of 255, so 60 is 153 of 255, as in After Effects; `colors`, up to eight colours `#rrggbb`, with `tolerance`, 0 to 255, starting at 0, used with Chosen colours: D-87 and D-88's choice exactly; `radius`, Glow Radius, 0 to 500 pixels, starting at 10, how far the light spreads; `intensity`, Glow Intensity, 0 to 10, starting at 1, how strong it is; `operation`, Glow Operation, Add (the default) or Screen; and `tint`, Glow Colours, empty for the glow's own colours, or one colour `#rrggbb` that all the light takes. Threshold, radius, intensity and tolerance can be keyed (D-68); each is held inside its range at each frame and none is rounded. **The method** is this program's own, built from document 21's Gaussian blur and D-88's colour test; nothing is ported, so no licence is taken on. OpenToonz's Glow and Bloom (`stdfx`, BSD-3) and F's Plugins (MIT) were read and are not used: OpenToonz's Glow takes its light from a second picture and blurs with a tent, and its Bloom glows the whole picture; neither is After Effects' model. **Steps:** (1) the pixels that glow, by threshold or by chosen colour, are kept, and every other pixel is emptied; (2) with a tint, each kept pixel takes the tint's colour at its own covering; (3) they are blurred by document 21's Gaussian at sigma radius / 3, so the light reaches `radius` pixels; (4) the blurred light is multiplied by the intensity, its covering too; (5) it is laid on the picture: Add adds the light, which is not cut off at white, and the covering adds up to full (FX-GLOW-011); Screen screens it on, never past white (FX-GLOW-012). This is After Effects' Composite Original set to On Top. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017), and the light grows the drawing's bounds by the radius, as Blur does, so a glow that spreads past the drawing's edge is kept when the drawing is moved (FX-GLOW-019). On an adjustment layer it glows the picture below. A draft preview scales the radius, as it does blur. **Where it differs from After Effects, on purpose:** it works in linear light, as every effect here does (document 21), where a default After Effects project mixes encoded colours, so the same numbers give a softer, brighter-edged light than there; the threshold is still read on encoded colours, so 60 selects the same pixels. Glow Based On chooses bright parts or chosen colours, where After Effects chooses colour or alpha, as the owner asked. Glow Colours is one tint, not After Effects' A and B colours with their looping. **Not in this decision:** Composite Original's Behind and None, Glow Dimensions (horizontal or vertical only), A and B colours, and a soft edge to the threshold. **Out of range.** A command with a number outside its range, more than eight colours, a colour or tint not written `#` and six hexadecimal digits, an operation other than add or screen, or a based-on other than bright or colors is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-GLOW-022 to 033). **Checks.** B-33b adds the effect to the core and a table that renders every FX-GLOW case against `Fixtures/glow/expected_glow.json`. B-33c adds it to the Effects panel and a playtest sheet on the owner's purple flame.

D-90 / Limits for the blur and exposure / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-25 by the owner ("works; proceed with limits")**, proposed the same day by the agent from the effects audit P-16 left open. **Why.** Two settings had no upper end. A Gaussian blur's `sigma_px` could be any size: sigma 10,000 asks for a kernel 60,001 pixels wide and a picture grown by 30,000 pixels on every side, which runs the machine out of memory and closes the window with the work unsaved. Exposure's `stops` could be any finite number: at 128 stops or more `2^e` is infinite as a 32-bit number, and a transparent pixel times infinity is not-a-number, which spreads through every layer drawn over it. **The rule.** `sigma_px` runs from 0 to 500 and `stops` from -20 to 20, both ends included. 500 is Glow's own radius limit (D-89) and more blur than any frame this project makes can show; 20 stops is a million times brighter or darker, far past any real exposure change. **A value on a limit** is an ordinary value and renders as document 21 says (FX-LIMIT-001 to 003). **A value past a limit** is D-46's invalid parameter, as a negative sigma already is: a command that would set it is refused with a sentence ("A Gaussian blur's sigma runs from 0 to 500, and this is 501.", "Exposure runs from -20 to 20 stops, and this is 21.") and changes nothing; a file that holds it is read, the effect is kept exactly as written and left out of every frame with `EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID` (FX-LIMIT-006 to 010). A keyed setting is D-68's: one key past a limit leaves the whole effect out, and an ease that overshoots between two keys in range is held at the limit (FX-LIMIT-004, 005). The refusal for a negative sigma now uses the same words as the one for too large a sigma. **It changes no existing fixture**: no fixture holds a sigma above 500 or an exposure past 20 stops. **The fixture came first:** `tools/limits_reference.py` renders the ten cases pixel by pixel through `tools/adjust_reference.py` and `tools/fxkey_reference.py`; document 25's FX-LIMIT-001 to 010 are its output, with their projects and drawings in `Fixtures/limits/`.

D-91 / Line recolour / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-25** by the owner's batch message of 2026-09-25, "knowing the expectation, let's do a batch of 1 thru 7 in your recommended order", the first of seven effects the agent listed and recommended in this order after Glow: line recolour, directional blur, select colour, line width, radial blur, bloom and colour key (D-91 to D-97). One picture in `verification/B-35a proposal/`. FX-RECOLOR-001 to 018 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-35. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It repaints the pixels of chosen colours in one new colour, keeping each pixel's own covering: a drawing's black line turned brown or red, as an animator's coloured line does, with an antialiased edge staying soft in the new colour. It is `core.line_recolor`, named Line Recolour in the Effects panel. **Settings:** `colors`, up to eight colours `#rrggbb`, with `tolerance`, 0 to 255, starting at 0: D-87 and D-88's choice exactly; and `new_color`, the colour they become, `#rrggbb`, starting at `#ff0000`. Tolerance can be keyed (D-68) and is held inside its range at each frame; colours cannot. With no colour chosen it changes nothing. **The method** is this program's own; nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017), with no growth of its bounds and nothing for a draft preview to scale; on an adjustment layer it recolours the picture below. **Not in this decision:** a separate colour per chosen colour, and keeping a line's shading (it takes one flat colour). **Out of range.** A command with a tolerance outside 0 to 255, more than eight colours, or a colour or new colour not written `#` and six hexadecimal digits is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-RECOLOR-012 to 018).

D-92 / Directional blur / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-25** by the owner's batch message of 2026-09-25, "knowing the expectation, let's do a batch of 1 thru 7 in your recommended order", the second of the seven (D-91 to D-97). One picture in `verification/B-36a proposal/`. FX-DIRBLUR-001 to 015 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-36. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It smears a layer along one direction, as a camera moving during the exposure does: each pixel becomes the plain average of samples taken along a line through it, for speed lines, a pan's blur and a fast move. It is `core.directional_blur`, named Directional Blur in the Effects panel. **Settings:** `direction`, in degrees clockwise from up, -3600 to 3600, starting at 0, so 0 streaks up and down and 90 left and right; and `length`, the whole streak in pixels, half on each side, 0 to 500, starting at 10. Both can be keyed (D-68) and are held inside their ranges at each frame. Length 0 changes nothing. **The method** is this program's own, modelled on After Effects' Directional Blur; nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017). Its bounds grow by half the length, rounded up, on every side, so a streak leaving the drawing's edge is kept; a draft preview scales the length as it does a blur's sigma (D-66). **Not in this decision:** a streak on one side only, and a weighting other than plain. **Out of range.** A command with a setting outside its range is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-DIRBLUR-012 to 015).

D-93 / Select colour / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-25** by the owner's batch message of 2026-09-25, "knowing the expectation, let's do a batch of 1 thru 7 in your recommended order", the third of the seven (D-91 to D-97). One picture in `verification/B-37a proposal/`. FX-SELECT-001 to 016 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-37. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It keeps the pixels of chosen colours and makes every other pixel transparent, or the reverse: a drawing's line alone, to treat on its own, or the drawing without its line. It is `core.select_color`, named Select Colour in the Effects panel. **Settings:** `colors`, up to eight colours `#rrggbb`, with `tolerance`, 0 to 255, starting at 0: D-87 and D-88's choice exactly; and `keep`, the word `chosen` or `others`, starting at `chosen`. Tolerance can be keyed (D-68) and is held inside its range at each frame; colours and keep cannot. With no colour chosen it changes nothing, whichever it keeps; with colours chosen that match nothing and keep `chosen`, the layer is empty. A kept pixel is the drawing's own, exactly, its covering included. **The method** is this program's own; nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017), with no growth of its bounds and nothing for a draft preview to scale. **Not in this decision:** a soft edge to the choice (a pixel is kept or not). **Out of range.** A command with a tolerance outside 0 to 255, more than eight colours, a colour not written `#` and six hexadecimal digits, or a keep other than the two words is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-SELECT-010 to 016).

D-94 / Line width / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-25** by the owner's batch message of 2026-09-25, "knowing the expectation, let's do a batch of 1 thru 7 in your recommended order", the fourth of the seven (D-91 to D-97). One picture in `verification/B-38a proposal/`. FX-WIDTH-001 to 019 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-38. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It thickens or thins a drawing's lines by a number of pixels, as a thicker or thinner pen would have drawn them. It is `core.line_width`, named Line Width in the Effects panel. **Settings:** `width`, -20 to 20 pixels, starting at 1, positive to thicken and negative to thin; `based_on`, the word `shape` or `colors`, starting at `shape`; and `colors` with `tolerance`, D-87 and D-88's choice exactly, used only when it is based on colours. Width and tolerance can be keyed (D-68) and are held inside their ranges at each frame. **On the shape** a positive width gives each pixel the covering and colour of the most covered pixel within the width, so the whole drawing grows; a negative width lowers each pixel's covering to the least covered within it, its own colour kept, so the drawing shrinks. **On colours** a positive width paints each pixel within the width of a chosen colour with the nearest chosen pixel, so only the line grows; a negative width gives each chosen pixel within the width of anything else the nearest such pixel, so the line thins. "Within the width" is every pixel whose centre is no further than the width; of equals, the nearest wins, then the one above, then the one to the left. Width 0, or colours with none chosen, changes nothing. **The method** is this program's own; nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017). A positive width grows its bounds by the width, rounded up, on every side; a draft preview scales the width (D-66). **Known limit:** it works in whole pixels, so thinning a line about two pixels wide on a slant leaves it dotted, as the picture shows; a smoother thinning is not in this decision. **Out of range.** A command with a width outside -20 to 20, a tolerance outside 0 to 255, a based-on other than the two words, more than eight colours, or a colour not written `#` and six hexadecimal digits is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-WIDTH-013 to 019).

D-95 / Radial blur / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-25** by the owner's batch message of 2026-09-25, "knowing the expectation, let's do a batch of 1 thru 7 in your recommended order", the fifth of the seven (D-91 to D-97). One picture in `verification/B-39a proposal/`. FX-RADIAL-001 to 018 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-39. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It smears a drawing round a centre, as a camera spinning or zooming during the exposure would. It is `core.radial_blur`, named Radial Blur in the Effects panel. **Settings:** `type`, the word `spin` or `zoom`, starting at `spin`; `amount`, 0 to 100, starting at 10, the arc in degrees for a spin and the stretch in per cent of the distance from the centre for a zoom; and `center`, two numbers, per cent of the drawing's width and height, starting at 50, 50, its middle, and allowed from -1000 to 1000 so the centre may sit off the drawing. Amount and centre can be keyed (D-68) and are held inside their ranges at each frame. **The rule.** Each pixel becomes the plain average of samples taken along the arc of the circle about the centre through it (spin), or along the line from the centre through it (zoom), half each way; the further a pixel is from the centre, the longer its smear. The samples are about a pixel apart along the smear, at most 256 of them. **The method** is this program's own, modelled on After Effects' Radial Blur; nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017), with the centre in the drawing's own size even after an effect above it has grown the layer. It does not grow the layer: nothing is drawn outside the drawing's edge. A draft preview changes nothing, as the amount is an angle or a share and the centre a share. **Known limits:** about one sample a pixel along the smear, so a thin line crossing it shows fine stripes, as the picture shows; and a smear cut off at the drawing's edge, as FX-RADIAL-010 shows. **Out of range.** A command with an amount outside 0 to 100, a centre number outside -1000 to 1000, or a type other than the two words is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-RADIAL-013 to 018).

D-96 / Bloom / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-25** by the owner's batch message of 2026-09-25, "knowing the expectation, let's do a batch of 1 thru 7 in your recommended order", the sixth of the seven (D-91 to D-97). One picture in `verification/B-40a proposal/`. FX-BLOOM-001 to 028 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-40. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It makes the brightest parts of a drawing flood with light, the way strong light blooms on film: a halo that is tight and bright close to them and wide and faint further out, and, if asked, streaks of light crossing it, as a star filter on a lens gives. It is `core.bloom`, named Bloom in the Effects panel. Glow (D-89) spreads light evenly to its radius; bloom keeps more of it close and lets a little reach further, and has the streaks. **Settings:** `threshold`, 0 to 100, starting at 80, how bright a part must be to bloom, tested exactly as glow's bright parts are; `radius`, 0 to 500 pixels, starting at 20, how far the halo reaches; `intensity`, 0 to 10, starting at 1; `streaks`, the word `none`, `cross` or `star`, starting at `none`; `length`, 0 to 500 pixels, starting at 60, how far each streak reaches each way; and `angle`, -3600 to 3600 degrees, starting at 0, clockwise from up as directional blur's direction is. The five numbers can be keyed (D-68) and are held inside their ranges at each frame. **The rule.** The light is each pixel bright enough, as it is. The halo is the plain average of four Gaussian blurs of the light, each half as wide as the one before, the widest reaching the radius. A cross is two streaks, at the angle and a quarter turn on; a star is four, at eighth turns; each streak is the light smeared along its line, strongest in the middle and fading to nothing at the length, and the streaks are averaged. Halo and streaks, times the intensity, are added onto the drawing, the covering stopping at full and the colour not cut off at white, as glow's Add. **The method** is this program's own, built from glow's test, document 21's blur and directional blur's line samples; OpenToonz's Bloom was read and not used; nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017); the layer grows by the radius, or by the length with streaks if that is more, so the light spreads past the drawing's edge. A draft preview scales the radius and the length with the preview. **Known limits:** a streak is as wide as the bright part it comes from, so a large bright area gives broad beams, not thin rays, as the picture shows; and a large radius or length on a large layer is slow, which P-17 measures. **Out of range.** A command with a number outside its range, or a streaks word other than the three, is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-BLOOM-020 to 028).

D-97 / Colour key / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-25** by the owner's batch message of 2026-09-25, "knowing the expectation, let's do a batch of 1 thru 7 in your recommended order", the last of the seven (D-91 to D-97). One picture in `verification/B-41a proposal/`, with the drawing it is made from beside it. FX-KEY-001 to 023 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-41. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It makes the pixels of chosen colours transparent, as a green screen is taken out from behind a figure, with a soft band where pixels near the colour go only part of the way: a shadow on the screen fades rather than cutting off. It is `core.color_key`, named Colour Key in the Effects panel. Select colour (D-93) keeps or removes a pixel whole; colour key has the soft band and can match by hue. **Settings:** `colors`, up to eight colours `#rrggbb`, as D-87's, starting with none; `tolerance`, 0 to 255, starting at 20; `softness`, 0 to 255, starting at 20; and `match`, the word `rgb` or `hue`, starting at `rgb`. Tolerance and softness can be keyed (D-68) and are held inside their ranges at each frame; colours and match cannot. **The rule.** A pixel's distance from a chosen colour is worked on its 8-bit red, green and blue, as D-88's choice is. With `rgb` it is the largest of the three channel differences, so at softness 0 exactly D-88's chosen pixels go. With `hue` it is the difference of the two colours' hues on the colour wheel, the short way round, half a turn counting as 255; brightness does not count, so a darker shadow of the screen's green goes with it, and a grey, which has no hue, is 255 from everything. Of several colours the nearest counts. A pixel at or within the tolerance goes; one further than the tolerance and the softness together stays as it is; between, its colour and covering are both multiplied by how far across the band it is. With no colour chosen it changes nothing. **The method** is this program's own, modelled on After Effects' Color Key; nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017), with no growth of its bounds and nothing for a draft preview to scale. **Known limits:** it takes out; it does not take the screen's green light off what stays (no spill suppression), and with `hue` a dark line with green spilt on it has the screen's hue and goes too, as the picture's fourth panel shows, where `rgb` keeps it. **Out of range.** A command with a tolerance or softness outside 0 to 255, more than eight colours, a colour not written `#` and six hexadecimal digits, or a match other than the two words is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-KEY-016 to 023).

D-98 / A running sum for Directional Blur and Bloom's streaks / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-25 by the owner ("accept d98, proceed")**, proposed by the agent the same day at the owner's word ("propose the running sum change"), after P-17 left these two the slowest effects on an opaque plate. Built as B-42. Four pictures and `measurements.md` in `verification/B-42a proposal/`. **A correction first.** When the agent offered this change it said a running sum only adds the same numbers in a different order, moving pixels by about 1 part in 10 million. That was wrong. D-92's samples are `length / ceil(length)` apart. At any direction but the four quarter turns, each pixel's samples fall between pixels in a different place, so no two pixels share a sample and there is nothing to keep a running total of. A running sum needs a rule whose samples pixels share, which is a change to the rule. **The rule proposed.** The picture is read along straight lines in the blur's direction, one pixel apart, each sampled where it crosses a column's centre, or a row's for a blur that is mostly up and down. Along a line, a running total gives every point's average over the blur's length with one addition and one subtraction, whatever the length. A pixel takes the straight mix of the two lines passing nearest above and below its centre. For Directional Blur the average along a line is flat over the length plus one sample spacing, with its ends softened over a pixel. Straight across or down, that gives D-92's numbers exactly at every odd whole length (FX-DIRBLUR-006 is unchanged). For Bloom the streak keeps its tent over whole columns. The halo and everything else in D-96 are unchanged. Document 21 has the rule in full. **What moves**, in screen levels of 255 on D-92's face drawing: direction 30, length 10, largest 39, with 0.9 % of pixels moving more than 3; direction 45, length 30, largest 60 and 0.4 %; direction 0, length 30, largest 3 and none; Bloom's star, angle 20, length 60, on glow's flame, largest 4 and none. The most is on one-pixel lines near the diagonals in short blurs, where the new rule is a little crisper, because it samples on each column's centre and D-92 samples between pixels. The full table is in `measurements.md`. **Fixtures.** On acceptance both references work D-98's rule and nothing else, and their values replace D-92's and D-96's in `expected_directional_blur.json` and `expected_bloom.json`; the replaced values are retired, kept in the repository's history at commit ca2be49, the proposal. 9 of the 15 FX-DIRBLUR cases move, the largest by 0.065 in working value; 005, 006 and 012 to 015 are unchanged. 5 of the 28 FX-BLOOM cases move (007, 008, 011, 016 and 019), the largest by 0.041; 009, the cross at 90, now equals 006 exactly, where it equalled it only to rounding. **One case the proposal missed:** FX-RADIAL-012 puts a directional blur (90, length 4) ahead of the radial blur, and `tools/radial_blur_reference.py` works it with the directional blur's reference, so it moves too, 138 pixels by at most 0.017; the other 17 FX-RADIAL cases are unchanged. All three tools' checks pass. Three of Directional Blur's claims are restated with the new figures: 3.875 / 5 for 4 / 5, 1 / 15 for 1 / 16, and the covering kept over columns 2 to 12. **Speed.** A throwaway prototype, `verification/B-42a proposal/timing_prototype.rs`, was run on the D-01 machine: rustc 1.89.0, `-C opt-level=3`, one thread, a 1920x1080 opaque plate, direction 30, the median of 5 runs. Length 100 took 1123.6 ms by D-92's rule and 76.7 ms by the proposed one (14.6x); length 10 took 114.8 ms and 66.8 ms (1.7x). The build uses all 24 threads, and its own before and after would come with B-42. Bloom's streaks were not timed. Its halo, about 90 ms alone, is untouched, so Bloom's star on an opaque plate, 340 ms now, cannot fall below that. **Accepted:** the fixtures are replaced first, then B-42 builds it and re-runs the B-36, B-39 and B-40 tables and P-17's harness.

D-99 / A drawing's effects run at draft size in Draft preview / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-27 by the owner ("2 - accept them all"), with every other decision then proposed (D-167).** It was **PROPOSED on 2026-09-25, and built and switched on in this build at the owner's "proceed with option 1 and 2"**, the first of two speed-ups offered after "what's explore performance/optimization/gpu-acceleration". It waits on the owner's look at the pictures and a try in the app. Twelve pictures and `measurements.md` in `verification/D-99 proposal/`, written by `tests/d99_draft_effects.rs`. **It changes Draft preview's pixels and nothing else.** Full quality and export are untouched, and no fixture moves: every fixture is checked at Full. **The change.** Draft preview shows a quarter of the width and height. Until now a drawn layer's effects ran on the full-size drawing and the result was shrunk with the layer. Now, at Draft, a drawn layer with at least one enabled effect is shrunk to a quarter first, the way `scale_plan` shrinks a layer, and its effects run on the small drawing. Every distance in pixels is divided by four as they run, as a draft already did for masks (D-67): blur sigma and size, glow and bloom radii, streak and blur lengths, line widths. Radial Blur's amount and centre are an angle or a share and need nothing. The effect's result is kept in P-11's cache under a key that includes the size it was made at, so a draft result is never shown at Full. **What moves**, in screen levels of 255, at frame 100 of the reference shot, effect on the whole-frame background: Gaussian Blur sigma 8, largest 8, with 0.3 % of pixels moving more than 3; Glow, largest 7 and 0.2 %; Directional Blur 30 / 40, largest 34 and 14.8 %; Bloom's star, largest 32 and 6.0 %; Radial Blur zoom 20, largest 51 and 9.7 %. On the small flat ball, none moves more than 0.5 % of pixels. The moving pixels are fine brush-stroke texture inside the blurred area, smoothed a little more; the shapes, sizes and edges of what the effect draws are the same. **Speed** on the D-01 machine (rustc 1.89.0, release, all threads; median of 5 whole frames with no cache): the frame with no effect takes 47.8 ms, most of it reading the four drawings. With the effect on the background, Bloom's star went from 188.5 to 62.4 ms and Radial Blur from 231.3 to 47.4 ms. The lighter effects' own cost, 7 to 19 ms before, is now under the noise of reading the files. **Not covered:** a shape, solid or adjustment layer with an effect still runs it at full size and then shrinks, as before; and the small drawing is not kept between frames, which costs about 2 to 3 ms to redo. **If refused,** the draft branch in `resolve_layer` comes out and Draft preview is again what it was, pixel for pixel.

D-100 / A GPU preview tier, started while there are thirteen effects rather than thirty / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-25 by the owner, road (a): "accept D-100 (a)"**. ADR-006 is amended to match and B-44 joins document 15. Proposed the same day at the owner's "now let's start focusing on performance for the engine/playback/timeline. if that also includes gpu-acceleration, let's get started before the complexity gets too big for the project to handle." **What it reopens.** ADR-006 builds no GPU renderer "until a measured result on a real shot on the reference machine shows the CPU path is too slow", and D-51 kept that on 2026-09-12 after P-14 found a live blur drag keeping up at draft. That escape clause is still not triggered: after P-18 the first playthrough at draft drops no frames on either fixture (`verification/P-18_read_ahead.md`). **The owner's reason is a different one, and it is sound: the cost of a second renderer grows with every effect built without it.** There are thirteen effects now; each new one built CPU-only is one more to port and match later. That is a scope decision rather than a measurement, so it is the owner's, and this entry is where it is made. **D-51's objection still stands and the proposal is shaped around it**: a GPU does not give the same bits as this CPU, so a GPU that drew exports would move every fixture from exact equality to a tolerance, on hardware that differs between cards and driver versions. **Two roads, from document 32 Tier 3.** (a) **A preview tier.** The CPU stays the only authority. Every fixture, every export and Full-quality checking stay on the CPU, byte-exact, exactly as today. The GPU draws only the viewer's picture, behind a switch, and a new kind of table checks it against the CPU over the fixture frames, with a difference picture for each. Anything the GPU cannot do yet, such as an effect not yet ported, is done on the CPU for that layer and handed to the card, and the frame log names each layer the CPU drew so the fallback is visible, not silent. (b) **GPU everywhere**, exports included, with the fixtures moving to tolerances. **Recommendation: (a).** Nothing the owner has already verified changes, a GPU mistake can only ever appear in the viewer, and a difference picture shows it. **What is already measured**, in `verification/P-07_gpu_distance.md`, on this machine's RTX 4070 Ti SUPER on 2026-09-10: on the H-01 frames the GPU and CPU composites differ by **one screen level of 255 at one pixel of four frames**, and under a deliberately hard rotation by one level at 519 of 2,073,600 pixels. Two design constraints come from the same page. The layer transform must be inverted on the CPU in f64 and handed over, because inverting a near-singular scale in the GPU's f32 lands 32 source pixels away. And moving one full working-precision frame onto the card and back costs 14.5 ms, a third of a 24 fps frame, so **the design keeps the drawings on the card between frames and brings back only the finished eight-bit picture** (0.5 MB at draft, 8 MB at Full), never the working-precision frame. **Proposed tolerance for the check:** no pixel more than 1 level of 255 from the CPU for compositing. Each effect declares and measures its own tolerance when it is ported, because a blur that adds its samples in a different order can drift further, and that is shown with pictures before it is accepted. **What a GPU will not speed up:** reading and decoding drawings from disk, most of the 47.8 ms of an uncached draft frame in D-99's table. It is the compositing and the effects that it would take over, which is where Full quality, heavy effects on opaque plates (Radial Blur 160 to 185 ms in `verification/P-17_effect_cost.md`) and drags at Full (52.8 ms a frame in P-14) spend their time. **The tool is wgpu**, the Rust GPU library P-07 used (Vulkan or DirectX 12 underneath). It is a large new dependency and makes the build longer. `spikes/p07_gpu` stays quarantined and nothing is copied from it; production code is written fresh. **Order of work if accepted**, each unit ending in its own comparison table, pictures and timings: first B-44, the GPU compositor for drawn layers (transform, opacity, blend modes, mattes), behind a Preview CPU / GPU switch that stays on CPU until the owner passes a playtest; then the effects one at a time, heaviest first: Radial Blur, Bloom, Directional Blur, then Gaussian Blur and Glow. Sending the picture straight to the screen instead of through the page is a later, separate question (document 33 warns it is integration work of its own). **Unchanged either way:** ADR-015's export, ADR-017's whole-layer effects, and every fixture. **Cost if accepted:** a second renderer kept matched for the life of the project. Every new effect then needs a GPU version or runs on the CPU in the GPU preview. The tolerance table is checked on this machine's card only. And ADR-006 in document 18 is amended to say a GPU preview tier is allowed and a GPU export is not. **Cost if declined:** nothing; performance work continues on the CPU.

D-101 / `GPU_PREVIEW_ON_CPU`: the viewer says when the graphics card did not draw a frame / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-27 by the owner ("2 - accept them all"), with every other decision then proposed (D-167).** It was **PROPOSED on 2026-09-25 by the agent while building B-44**, which cannot be built without it. **The gap.** Document 28 has two GPU identifiers, `GPU_BACKEND_FAILED` and `GPU_OUT_OF_MEMORY`, both ERROR and both written for a production GPU path that refuses a request. D-100 (a) built no such path: the card draws only the viewer's picture, and when it cannot, the CPU draws the same frame, which is always possible and always correct. Nothing is refused, so an ERROR would be wrong, but a quiet switch to the CPU would break the rule against silent fallback. **The proposal.** One identifier, `GPU_PREVIEW_ON_CPU`, raised on the frame the CPU drew instead, with the reason in its sentence. It is INFO when the reason is the project's (an adjustment layer, which D-66 keeps on the CPU, or a picture larger than the card's texture limit) and WARNING when it is the card's (a failed draw, or running out of memory). Its words go into the session log (P-19) and the frame's reply, and the viewer's label reads "drawn on CPU, not GPU". **What it does not change.** Document 28's table of core identifiers and its count stay as they are; `GPU_BACKEND_FAILED` and `GPU_OUT_OF_MEMORY` stay unbuilt, for a GPU path that exports, which nothing plans. Proof: `verification/B-44_gpu_preview_table.md` and `verification/B-12b_diagnostic_catalogue.md`.

D-102 / The graphics card paints the viewer's picture into the window, under the page / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-27 by the owner ("2 - accept them all"), with every other decision then proposed (D-167).** It was **PROPOSED on 2026-09-26 by the agent, and built the same day as B-45 at the owner's "proceed with the native viewer surface"**, after the owner's "if you need to change the app's architecture to further support/have native gpu-acceleration, say the word." **The gap.** B-44 has the card draw the picture and then copy it back so the page can show it: at Full, 8 MB back from the card and 8 MB again into the page for every frame. That round trip, not the drawing, is what kept B-44 from being faster than the CPU. ADR-004 already names the answer as its fallback: "a native rendering surface hosted inside the web shell". **The proposal.** With the switch on GPU, the card paints the picture straight into the window, under a see-through page. The page tells the card where the picture lies and what the page had painted under it (its background colours and the checkerboard), in window pixels. Only those areas of the page become see-through, so everything else still draws on top. A zoom or a scroll sends only the new place. If the card cannot paint the window, it stops for the session, the status line and the switch's tooltip say why, and the picture goes to the page as in B-44: no silent fallback. **What it does not change.** Exports, fixtures and the CPU picture are untouched. D-100's tolerance applies to what the card draws, and `verification/B-44_gpu_preview_table.md` is unchanged. **What it costs.** Text in the window is smoothed in grey rather than with ClearType while the card paints, because Windows cannot use ClearType over a see-through page. At columns where a screen pixel falls exactly between two picture pixels, the card and the page may take neighbouring pixels, since the page is not consistent about which one it takes. Proof: `verification/B-45_native_viewer.md`, whose comparisons match exactly when zoomed to 300% and whose playback at Full skips no frames where B-44 skipped 82 in 8 seconds. **B-45's playtest passed on 2026-09-26: "works great!"** The decision itself stays proposed until the owner accepts it by name.

D-103 / Radial Blur on the card is held to 1 level of 255 / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-27 by the owner ("2 - accept them all"), with every other decision then proposed (D-167).** It was **PROPOSED on 2026-09-26 by the agent, and built the same day as B-46 at the owner's "let's proceed with gpu-acceleration on the effects"**. D-100 has each effect declare and measure its own tolerance when it moves to the card, and show it in pictures before it is accepted. **The proposal:** Radial Blur keeps compositing's tolerance, no channel of any pixel more than 1 level of 255 from the CPU's picture. **The measurement:** `verification/B-46_gpu_radial_table.md` covers every frame of FX-RADIAL-001 to 012, and frames 0, 100 and 239 of the reference shot with three Radial Blurs, at Full and Draft. The three blurs include the most spin there is, which takes 256 samples a pixel. All are within 1 level. The worst, frame 0 at Full, differs at 20,539 of 2,073,600 pixels, by 1 level each, scattered as rounding noise. Its pictures are in `verification/B-46 pictures/`. The card takes the same samples as the CPU, from the same table of turns. The differences come from two places: it reads the drawing as the card holds it, in half precision (B-44b), and it adds the samples in single precision rather than double. **What it does not change:** exports and fixtures stay on the CPU, byte-exact, and a frame the card cannot draw is drawn by the CPU exactly as before. **If refused:** the switch to GPU leaves Radial Blur to the CPU again, as in B-45, and nothing else moves. **The owner's B-46 playtest passed on 2026-09-26 ("works; proceed to next").** That passes the unit; the decision itself stays proposed until the owner accepts it by name.

D-104 / Bloom on the card is held to 1 level of 255, and starts from the drawing in full precision / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-27 by the owner ("2 - accept them all"), with every other decision then proposed (D-167).** It was **PROPOSED on 2026-09-26 by the agent, and built the same day as B-47 at the owner's "works; proceed to next"**. D-100 has each effect declare and measure its own tolerance when it moves to the card, and show it in pictures before it is accepted. **The proposal:** Bloom keeps compositing's tolerance, no channel of any pixel more than 1 level of 255 from the CPU's picture. To meet it, a drawing a Bloom starts from goes to the card as the CPU holds it, four 32-bit numbers a pixel, not in B-44b's half precision. **Why that is needed:** Bloom first keeps only the pixels at least as bright as the threshold. Half precision moves some pixels from one side of the threshold to the other, and each one moved adds or loses a whole halo and its streaks. Built first with half precision, the reference shot with three Blooms was up to 9 levels off at Full and 40 at Draft. With full precision it is within 1. **The cost:** such a drawing takes twice the card's memory, sixteen bytes a pixel against eight. **Double precision:** the streaks keep running totals over long lines, which the CPU keeps in double precision, and the card does the same. A card that cannot (Vulkan calls it `SHADER_F64`; this machine's card can, through Vulkan) has frames with a Bloom drawn by the CPU, with an Info message saying why. That path has not been seen, because this machine's card never takes it. **The measurement:** `verification/B-47_gpu_bloom_table.md` covers every frame of FX-BLOOM-001 to 028, and frames 0, 100 and 239 of the reference shot with three Blooms, at Full and Draft: 288 of 288 checks pass. On every fixture frame the card's picture is the same bytes as the CPU's. The worst, the reference shot's frame 0 at Full, differs at 2,640 of 2,073,600 pixels, by 1 level each. Its pictures are in `verification/B-47 pictures/`. **What it does not change:** exports and fixtures stay on the CPU, byte-exact, and a frame the card cannot draw is drawn by the CPU exactly as before. **If refused:** the switch to GPU leaves Bloom to the CPU again, as in B-46, and nothing else moves.

D-105 / The preview draws on the card whenever it can, and its memory is sized to the machine / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-26 by the owner ("accept D-105"), before it was built, and built the same day as B-48**. Raised by the owner: "can we have the gpu/cpu adaptively switch when needbe? I don't want to have to switch to draw on either every time. also I would like the option to allocate ram/vram if able to, or toggle to be adaptive." **(a) Draw on: Auto, GPU or CPU.** It amends D-100 (a), whose switch started on the CPU at every launch. The viewer's switch becomes a choice of three, kept with the window's preferences, and a new window starts on Auto. Auto draws on the card whenever it can. A frame the card refuses is drawn by the CPU, as D-100 already says. A frame the card fails makes Auto give the card up for the rest of the session, with one sentence saying so. GPU tries the card on every frame, even after it fails. CPU never uses the card. **Why no switching by timing:** the card is faster on every measured frame (`verification/B-48_memory_timing_table.md`), and a preview that changed processor from frame to frame would change its picture by D-100's 1 level from frame to frame. Exports stay on the CPU whatever is chosen (ADR-006). **(b) Memory: Automatic or Custom**, in Preferences, the window's and never a project's. Each amount is a most, not a reservation. Automatic gives the viewer's cache a quarter of the machine's memory, never less than D-40's 1 GiB, split as D-40's is: seven sixteenths for effect results. The card gets half its memory, as B-44b set it. Custom may give the cache from 1 GiB to three quarters of the machine's memory, and the card from 1 GiB to 85% of its memory. This is document 27's "configurable cache budget after measuring the reference machine". `CelCache::viewer()`, the 1 GiB every earlier table measured, is kept for those tables so they still compare. **The measurement:** on this machine, 66.1 GB, Automatic is 16.5 GB. The reference shot with B-47's three Blooms needs about 3.3 GB. With 1 GiB it threw away each frame what the next one needed. Playing it again at Full took 171 ms a frame on the CPU and 28 on the card; with Automatic it takes 17 and 3.5. The pictures are the same bytes with either amount (`verification/B-48_memory_table.md`). **What it does not change:** exports, fixtures and every picture. **If refused:** the switch goes back to two settings starting on the CPU, and the cache to 1 GiB.

D-106 / Directional Blur on the card is held to 1 level of 255 / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-27 by the owner ("2 - accept them all"), with every other decision then proposed (D-167).** It was **PROPOSED on 2026-09-26 by the agent, and built the same day as B-49 at the owner's "proceed"**. D-100 has each effect declare and measure its own tolerance when it moves to the card, and show it in pictures before it is accepted. **The proposal:** Directional Blur keeps compositing's tolerance, no channel of any pixel more than 1 level of 255 from the CPU's picture. **How the card does it:** the same lines and running totals as the CPU (D-98), kept in double precision as B-47's streaks are, so it needs the same `SHADER_F64`, and a card without it has such frames drawn by the CPU with an Info message. Unlike Bloom (D-104), the drawing goes to the card in B-44b's half precision: a blur averages its samples and has no threshold for a rounding to cross. **The measurement:** `verification/B-49_gpu_directional_table.md` covers every frame of FX-DIRBLUR-001 to 015, and frames 0, 100 and 239 of the reference shot with three Directional Blurs, at Full and Draft: 158 of 158 checks pass. The fixtures differ from the CPU at no more than 2 pixels a frame, by 1 level each. The worst, the reference shot's frame 100 at Full, differs at 14,674 of 2,073,600 pixels (0.7%), by 1 level each. Its pictures are in `verification/B-49 pictures/`. **What it does not change:** exports and fixtures stay on the CPU, byte-exact, and a frame the card cannot draw is drawn by the CPU exactly as before. **If refused:** Directional Blur goes back to the CPU, as in B-48, and nothing else moves.

D-107 / Gaussian Blur on the card is held to 1 level of 255 / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-27 by the owner ("2 - accept them all"), with every other decision then proposed (D-167).** It was **PROPOSED on 2026-09-26 by the agent, and built the same day as B-50 at the owner's "proceed with gaussian blur and glow"**. D-100 has each effect declare and measure its own tolerance when it moves to the card, and show it in pictures before it is accepted. **The proposal:** Gaussian Blur keeps compositing's tolerance, no channel of any pixel more than 1 level of 255 from the CPU's picture. **How the card does it:** across and then down with the CPU's own weights, each pixel adding its taps in the CPU's order, in the pass B-47's Bloom already blurs with. The drawing goes to the card in B-44b's half precision, as for Directional Blur (D-106). The pass is in the same part of the card's program as Bloom's double-precision streaks, so a card without `SHADER_F64` has such frames drawn by the CPU with an Info message. **The measurement:** `verification/B-50_gpu_gaussian_table.md` covers every frame of FX-FXK-006 and FX-PRE-002, and frames 0, 100 and 239 of the reference shot with three Gaussian Blurs, at Full and Draft: 24 of 24 checks pass. FX-FXK-006 is the same bytes on both. The worst, the reference shot's frame 0 at Full, differs at 20,915 of 2,073,600 pixels (1.0%), by 1 level each. Its pictures are in `verification/B-50 pictures/`. The other fixtures with a Gaussian Blur have it on an adjustment layer, which the card does not draw. **What it does not change:** exports and fixtures stay on the CPU, byte-exact, and a frame the card cannot draw is drawn by the CPU exactly as before. **If refused:** Gaussian Blur goes back to the CPU, as in B-49, and nothing else moves.

D-108 / Glow on the card is held to 1 level of 255 / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-27 by the owner ("2 - accept them all"), with every other decision then proposed (D-167).** It was **PROPOSED on 2026-09-26 by the agent, and built the same day as B-51 at the owner's "proceed with gaussian blur and glow"**. D-100 has each effect declare and measure its own tolerance when it moves to the card, and show it in pictures before it is accepted. **The proposal:** Glow keeps compositing's tolerance, no channel of any pixel more than 1 level of 255 from the CPU's picture. **How the card does it:** it finds what glows as the CPU does, on each pixel's 8-bit colour (bright parts by Bloom's test, or chosen colours within the tolerance), takes the tint if there is one, blurs the light across and then down with the CPU's weights and order, and lays it on by Add or Screen. It uses the passes of B-47's Bloom. The drawing goes to the card in full precision, as for Bloom (D-104), because a threshold decides what glows. A card without `SHADER_F64` has such frames drawn by the CPU with an Info message. A Glow at intensity 0 or with nothing that glows is not sent to the card. **The measurement:** `verification/B-51_gpu_glow_table.md` covers every frame of FX-GLOW-001 to 033, and frames 0, 100 and 239 of the reference shot with three Glows, at Full and Draft: 338 of 338 checks pass. All 33 fixtures are the same bytes on both. The worst, the reference shot's frame 0 at Full, differs at 1,981 of 2,073,600 pixels (0.1%), by 1 level each. Its pictures are in `verification/B-51 pictures/`. **What it does not change:** exports and fixtures stay on the CPU, byte-exact, and a frame the card cannot draw is drawn by the CPU exactly as before. **If refused:** Glow goes back to the CPU, as in B-50, and nothing else moves.

D-109 / Repeat Edge Pixels for the three blurs / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-27 by the owner ("2 - accept them all"), with every other decision then proposed (D-167).** It was **PROPOSED on 2026-09-26 by the agent, and built at the owner's "proceed, add to other blurs if needed"**, after the owner asked "how do we get radial blur to not cause transparency from the edges". FX-EDGES-001 to 012 in document 25 are its fixtures. **It adds one setting and changes no existing fixture.** **The problem.** Each blur mixes every pixel with pixels round it. At the edge of a layer some of those lie outside it, and document 21 counts them as transparent. On a character that makes no difference, because a character's edges are already empty. On a picture that fills the frame, a background plate, the edges fade into see-through: D-95 lists this for Radial Blur as the smear cut off at the drawing's edge, and Gaussian and Directional Blur fade the same way. **What it does.** Gaussian Blur (shown as Blur), Directional Blur and Radial Blur each get a switch, **Edges**: **Transparent**, the rule each has now, or **Repeat Edge Pixels**, After Effects' name for the same thing. With Repeat Edge Pixels, a blur reaching past the edge takes the edge pixel instead, so a picture that fills the frame stays solid to its edges. The layer then does not grow, because nothing past the edge is drawn. **In the file** it is `edges`, the word `transparent` or `repeat`. A file without it means `transparent`, and `transparent` is not written, so every existing project opens and saves exactly as before. Any other word is kept as written and the blur is left out with a warning, as D-46 does for every word setting. **It starts at Transparent** for a blur added now, too, so nothing already made or about to be made changes unless the switch is thrown. **Not given the switch:** Bloom and Glow, which add light rather than smear the picture, and whose light fading at the edge is right; Selective Colour Blur, which only ever reads the chosen pixels inside the drawing; and every other effect, which reads nothing outside the drawing. **The rule** is in document 21, "Repeat edge pixels". **The method** is this program's own; nothing is ported. **On the card** (D-100) the same switch is done by the card, held to the tolerance each blur already has there (D-103, D-106, D-107). **If refused:** the switch is taken out, the fixtures FX-EDGES-001 to 012 are retired, and a blur's edges fade as before.

D-110 / Radial Blur's zoom smears outward, as After Effects' does / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-27 by the owner ("2 - accept them all"), with every other decision then proposed (D-167).** It was **PROPOSED on 2026-09-26 by the agent, and built at the owner's "improve the zoom/radial blur to behave like AE"**, where the owner named the direction of the streaks as what differs. **It changes four existing fixtures:** FX-RADIAL-002, 005 and 007, and FX-EDGES-008. Their first values are retired, and document 25 says by how much each moved. **The problem.** D-95's zoom took each pixel's samples half each way along the line through the centre: at amount 100, from half the pixel's distance from the centre out to one and a half times it. So the picture smeared inward as much as outward. After Effects' zoom, in Adobe's words, "blurs radially outward from the center point": things streak away from the centre, as when a camera zooms in during the exposure. **What it does.** A zoom now takes each pixel's samples only between the pixel and the centre, so every edge streaks outward, away from the centre, and nothing streaks inward. **Amount keeps its meaning**, the length of the smear in per cent of the distance from the centre: at 100 a pixel samples all the way from the centre to itself. **Spin is unchanged.** **What it changes in a project:** a project made before with a zoom looks different, its streaks now going one way only; nothing else changes. Because every sample lies between the pixel and the centre, a zoom about a centre inside the drawing no longer fades at the drawing's edges even with Edges left at Transparent (D-109). **The rule** is in document 21, "Radial blur". **The method** is this program's own; nothing is ported, and Adobe publishes no formula, so it matches After Effects in direction, not pixel for pixel. **On the card** (D-100) the card does the same, held to D-103's 1 level of 255. **If refused:** the zoom goes back to half each way, the four fixtures go back to their first values, and nothing else moves.

D-111 / Curves / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-26** by the owner's batch message of 2026-09-26, "after this, and listing the 10 recommended effects to build in one batch, proceed with said batch", the first of the ten effects the agent listed and recommended (D-111 to D-120). One picture in `verification/B-54a proposal/`. FX-CURVES-001 to 020 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-54. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It regrades a drawing's colours through tone curves, as a colourist bends a curve to add contrast, lift the shadows or push one channel toward a colour: one curve for all three channels and one each for red, green and blue. It is `core.curves`, named Curves in the Effects panel. **Settings:** `master`, `red`, `green` and `blue`, each a list of 2 to 16 points `[in, out]`, both 0 to 255 on the scale of a colour as a drawing program holds it, with `in` strictly increasing; each starts as the straight line `[[0, 0], [255, 255]]`. The curves are lists and cannot be keyed. **The rule.** A pixel that shows is taken to its straight colour through the sRGB curve, each channel on 0 to 255. Each channel goes first through its own curve, then through the master, and the result is held inside 0 to 255; the colour comes back to linear at the pixel's own covering, which does not change. A curve is the natural cubic spline through its points, which is the straight line for two points, and outside its first and last points it stays flat at their values. A spline that swings above 255 or below 0 between points is held there. A pixel that does not show is left as it is, so an inverting curve leaves the empty space empty rather than white. With all four curves the default it changes nothing. **The method** is this program's own, modelled on After Effects' Curves; nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017), with no growth of its bounds and nothing for a draft preview to scale. **Not in this decision:** curves on the alpha channel, curves by hue or luminance, points that are keyed, and an on-screen curve editor beyond entering points; a later decision adds any of them. **Out of range.** A command with a curve of fewer than two or more than sixteen points, a value outside 0 to 255, an `in` that does not strictly increase, or a point that is not two numbers is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-CURVES-015 to 020).

D-112 / Levels / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-26** by the owner's batch message of 2026-09-26, "after this, and listing the 10 recommended effects to build in one batch, proceed with said batch", the second of the ten effects the agent listed and recommended (D-111 to D-120). One picture in `verification/B-55a proposal/`. FX-LEVELS-001 to 024 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-55. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It sets a drawing's darkest and lightest tones and bends the middle between them, as the levels of a photograph are set: it can deepen a washed-out drawing, soften one that is too hard, lighten or darken its middle tones, invert it, or cut it to a threshold. It is `core.levels`, named Levels in the Effects panel. Curves (D-111) can bend tones any way; levels does the common five-number job directly. **Settings:** `input_black`, 0 to 255, starting at 0; `input_white`, 0 to 255, starting at 255; `gamma`, 0.1 to 10, starting at 1; `output_black`, 0 to 255, starting at 0; and `output_white`, 0 to 255, starting at 255, all on the scale of a colour as a drawing program holds it. All five can be keyed (D-68) and are held inside their ranges at each frame. **The rule.** A pixel that shows is taken to its straight colour through the sRGB curve, each channel on 0 to 255. Each channel is placed on the input range, input black counting as 0 and input white as 1, and held inside 0 to 1; raised to the power 1 / gamma, so a gamma above 1 lightens the middle and one below darkens it; then laid on the output range. The colour comes back to linear at the pixel's own covering, which does not change.
