An input white below the input black, or an output black above the output white, inverts; an input white equal to the input black is a threshold, where a channel at or above it becomes the output white and one below the output black. A pixel that does not show is left as it is. At its starting settings it changes nothing. **The method** is this program's own, modelled on After Effects' Levels; nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017), with no growth of its bounds and nothing for a draft preview to scale. **Not in this decision:** levels per channel or on the alpha channel, a histogram, and automatic levels; a later decision adds any of them. **Out of range.** A command with a black or white outside 0 to 255 or a gamma outside 0.1 to 10 is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one, or a key that does, keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-LEVELS-018 to 024).

D-113 / Hue/Saturation / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-26** by the owner's batch message of 2026-09-26, "after this, and listing the 10 recommended effects to build in one batch, proceed with said batch", the third of the ten effects the agent listed and recommended (D-111 to D-120). One picture in `verification/B-56a proposal/`. FX-HUESAT-001 to 023 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-56. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It turns every colour of a drawing round the colour wheel, makes the colours more or less vivid, and lightens or darkens them, all at once: a whole palette shifted for a night scene, a flashback greyed out, a character's colours washed toward white. It is `core.hue_saturation`, named Hue/Saturation in the Effects panel. **Settings:** `hue`, -180 to 180 degrees, starting at 0; `saturation`, -100 to 100, starting at 0; and `lightness`, -100 to 100, starting at 0. All three can be keyed (D-68) and are held inside their ranges at each frame. **The method.** Each shown pixel's straight colour through the sRGB curve is read as hue, saturation and lightness (HSL), the hue worked as colour key's is (D-97). The hue setting is added to the hue, round the wheel, so past 360 comes back to 0 and below 0 comes back from 360. The saturation is multiplied by 1 plus the setting over 100 and held inside 0 and 1, so -100 greys everything and +100 doubles it. Above 0 the lightness moves that share of the way toward white; below 0, toward black, so +100 is white and -100 black. The colour is then turned back into red, green and blue by the standard HSL rule. A grey has no hue and no saturation, so hue and saturation leave it grey; the covering is kept, so a soft edge stays soft; a pixel that does not show stays as it is. With all three at 0 it changes nothing. The method is this program's own, modelled on After Effects' Hue/Saturation; nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017), with no growth of its bounds and nothing for a draft preview to scale. **Not in this decision:** After Effects' colorize option, its per-range (reds, yellows, greens and so on) channel control, and a hue shift of more than half a turn, which is the same as a shift the other way. **Out of range.** A command with a hue outside -180 to 180, or a saturation or lightness outside -100 to 100, is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-HUESAT-018 to 023); a setting that is not a number at all is a file of the wrong shape, refused as every effect's is.

D-114 / Gradient / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-26** by the owner's batch message of 2026-09-26, "after this, and listing the 10 recommended effects to build in one batch, proceed with said batch", the fourth of the ten effects the agent listed and recommended (D-111 to D-120). One picture in `verification/B-57a proposal/`. FX-GRAD-001 to 022 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-57. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It lays a colour gradient over a cel, the paraffin (パラ) of anime finishing: a wash that runs from one colour to another across the drawing, darkening, lightening or tinting it, as a sky-lit top and a shaded bottom are laid over a figure. It is `core.gradient`, named Gradient in the Effects panel. It touches only the pixels that show, and keeps each one's covering, so the wash never spills past the cel and a soft line edge stays soft. **Settings:** `shape`, the word `linear` or `radial`, starting at `linear`; `start` and `end`, two numbers each, per cent of the drawing's width and height as Radial Blur's centre is, starting at 50, 0 (the top middle) and 50, 100 (the bottom middle), each allowed from -1000 to 1000 so a point may sit off the drawing; `start_color` and `end_color`, `#rrggbb` as D-87's, starting at `#ffffff` and `#6450a0`; `start_opacity` and `end_opacity`, 0 to 100, starting at 0 and 50; and `blend`, the word `normal`, `multiply`, `screen` or `add`, starting at `multiply`. The two points and the two opacities can be keyed (D-68) and are held inside their ranges at each frame; the colours and the words cannot. **The rule.** Each pixel that shows finds how far along the gradient it lies, from 0 at the start to 1 at the end: along the line from the start to the end for `linear`, or its distance from the start over the distance from the start to the end for `radial`, held between 0 and 1, and 1 everywhere when the two points are the same. The colour there is mixed between the two colours as they are written (encoded values), and the opacity between the two opacities. The pixel's own colour is then moved toward the blend of itself and that colour by the opacity: the colour itself for `normal`, the two multiplied for `multiply`, the screen of the two for `screen`, the two added for `add`. **The method** is this program's own, modelled on After Effects' Gradient Ramp laid over a layer with a blending mode; nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017), with the points in the drawing's own size even after an effect above it has grown the layer. It does not grow the layer. A draft preview changes nothing, as the points are shares of the drawing. **Known limits:** two colours only; and `add` is not held below 1, so on a light cel it can brighten past white, as a wash of light does (the fixtures' `add` case, FX-GRAD-004, stays below it). **Out of range.** A command with an opacity outside 0 to 100, a point number outside -1000 to 1000, a colour not written `#` and six hexadecimal digits, or a shape or blend other than its words is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-GRAD-016 to 022).

D-115 / Drop shadow / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-26** by the owner's batch message of 2026-09-26, "after this, and listing the 10 recommended effects to build in one batch, proceed with said batch", the fifth of the ten effects the agent listed and recommended (D-111 to D-120). One picture in `verification/B-58a proposal/`. FX-SHADOW-001 to 023 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-58. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It lays a shadow of the drawing's own shape behind it, moved a distance in a direction and softened, as a cel lifted off the background casts one. It is `core.drop_shadow`, named Drop Shadow in the Effects panel. The shadow goes behind the drawing: where the drawing covers a pixel fully the shadow does not show, where it covers part of one (an antialiased edge) the shadow shows through the rest, and where the drawing is empty the shadow is all there is. **Settings:** `color`, a colour `#rrggbb` as D-87's, starting at `#000000`; `opacity`, 0 to 100 per cent, starting at 50; `direction`, -3600 to 3600 degrees clockwise from up, as Directional Blur's, starting at 135, down and to the right; `distance`, 0 to 1000 pixels, starting at 5; and `softness`, 0 to 500 pixels, starting at 0. The numbers can be keyed (D-68) and are held inside their ranges at each frame; the colour cannot. **The rule.** The drawing's covering is blurred by document 21's Gaussian blur at sigma softness / 3, so the softness is the blur's reach in pixels. The shadow at a pixel is that blurred covering read `distance` pixels back against the direction by document 21's bilinear sample, times the opacity: moved a whole number of pixels straight across or down it is the covering moved exactly, and moved slantwise or by part of a pixel it is spread over the pixels it falls between. Its colour is the chosen colour at that covering, and it goes behind the drawing as one picture goes behind another. At distance 0 and softness 0 the shadow sits exactly behind the drawing and shows only through its soft edges; at opacity 0 nothing changes. **The method** is this program's own, modelled on After Effects' Drop Shadow; nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017). Its bounds grow by the distance, rounded up, and the blur's reach on every side, at opacity 0 too, so a shadow falling past the drawing's edge is kept when the drawing is moved (FX-SHADOW-016); a draft preview scales the distance and the softness (D-66). **Not in this decision:** After Effects' Shadow Only, which shows the shadow without the drawing; Photoshop's spread, which fattens the shape before the blur; an inner shadow; and a shadow whose direction follows the composition's light or the layer's rotation, since it runs before the transform and so turns with the drawing. **Out of range.** A command with an opacity outside 0 to 100, a direction outside -3600 to 3600, a distance outside 0 to 1000, a softness outside 0 to 500, or a colour not written `#` and six hexadecimal digits is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one, written or at a key, keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-SHADOW-018 to 023).

D-116 / Lens blur / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-26** by the owner's batch message of 2026-09-26, "after this, and listing the 10 recommended effects to build in one batch, proceed with said batch", the sixth of the ten effects the agent listed and recommended (D-111 to D-120). One picture in `verification/B-59a proposal/`. FX-LENS-001 to 018 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-59. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It blurs a drawing as an out-of-focus lens does: each pixel becomes the plain average of every pixel within a circle round it, a flat disc rather than Gaussian Blur's bell, so a small bright spot spreads into an even round patch with a firm edge, where a Gaussian blur leaves a soft glow brightest in the middle. It is `core.lens_blur`, named Lens Blur in the Effects panel. **Settings:** `radius`, the circle's radius in pixels, 0 to 200, starting at 10; and `edges`, the word `transparent` or `repeat`, starting at `transparent`, as D-109's. The radius can be keyed (D-68) and is held inside its range at each frame; edges cannot. A radius under 1 takes each pixel alone and changes nothing. **The rule.** The circle is every whole-pixel step (dx, dy) with dx squared plus dy squared no more than the radius squared: 5 pixels, a plus, at radius 1; the 3 by 3 square at 1.5; 21 at 2.5; 49 at 4. The pixel becomes the plain average of the pixels at those steps, colour and covering alike. With `transparent` a step off the drawing counts as empty, so the edges fade and the drawing grows; with `repeat` a step off it takes the nearest edge pixel, so a picture that fills the frame stays solid to its edges. **The method** is this program's own, modelled on After Effects' Camera Lens Blur with a round iris; nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017). With `transparent` its bounds grow by the radius, rounded up, on every side, so the blur spreading past the drawing's edge is kept; with `repeat` they do not grow. A draft preview scales the radius as it does a blur's sigma (D-66). **Not in this decision:** an iris of another shape (blades, rotation), bright highlights blooming into brighter discs, and a depth map to vary the blur across the picture. **Known limit:** a large radius on a large layer is slow, as each pixel averages the whole circle. **Out of range.** A command with a radius outside 0 to 200, or edges other than the two words, is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-LENS-014 to 018).

D-117 / Rim light / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-26** by the owner's batch message of 2026-09-26, "after this, and listing the 10 recommended effects to build in one batch, proceed with said batch", the seventh of the ten effects the agent listed and recommended (D-111 to D-120). One picture in `verification/B-60a proposal/`. FX-RIM-001 to 028 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-60. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It lights the edge of a drawing that faces a light, as a back light catches the rim of a figure in anime: a band of light along the side toward the light, as deep as the width, fading at its inner edge. It is `core.rim_light`, named Rim Light in the Effects panel. **Settings:** `color`, the light's colour `#rrggbb`, as D-87's, starting at `#ffffff`; `direction`, where the light comes from, in degrees clockwise from up as directional blur's, -3600 to 3600, starting at 45, the upper right; `width`, how deep the rim reaches in pixels, 0 to 100, starting at 3; `softness`, how soft its inner edge is, in pixels, 0 to 100, starting at 1; `intensity`, 0 to 100, starting at 100; and `blend`, the word `normal`, `add`, `screen` or `multiply`, starting at `normal`. The four numbers can be keyed (D-68) and are held inside their ranges at each frame; colour and blend cannot. **The rule.** A pixel is lit by how far the point `width` pixels from it toward the light is off the drawing: the drawing's covering is blurred a little by the softness, and the rim is one less that blurred covering there. The pixel's colour moves toward the lit colour by the rim times the intensity: the light's colour itself (normal), the two added (add), screened, or multiplied. Its covering is kept, and a pixel that does not show is left exactly as it is. Width 0 lights only where the drawing's own covering is less than full, its soft edges. Intensity 0 changes nothing. **The method** is this program's own, modelled on how compositors build a rim light in After Effects from a shifted matte; nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017), with no growth of its bounds: it only changes pixels that show. A draft preview scales the width and the softness (D-66). **Known limit:** a separate part of the drawing within the width toward the light shades the rim, as it would a real light (FX-RIM-003's red dot); and the rim follows the drawing's outline only, not lines drawn inside it. **Not in this decision:** a light from a point rather than a direction, and a rim that follows the inner lines. **Out of range.** A command with a number outside its range, a blend other than the four words, or a colour not written `#` and six hexadecimal digits is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-RIM-022 to 028).

D-118 / Outline / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-26** by the owner's batch message of 2026-09-26, "after this, and listing the 10 recommended effects to build in one batch, proceed with said batch", the eighth of the ten effects the agent listed and recommended (D-111 to D-120). One picture in `verification/B-61a proposal/`. FX-OUTLINE-001 to 020 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-61. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It draws a band of colour round the drawing's shape, behind it, as an anime cel's outer line or a sticker's white border is. It is `core.outline`, named Outline in the Effects panel. Where the drawing covers a pixel fully the band does not show, where it covers part of one (an antialiased edge) the band shows through the rest, and any empty pixel near enough to the drawing, a hole inside it too, takes the band. **Settings:** `color`, a colour `#rrggbb` as D-87's, starting at `#ffffff`; `width`, 0 to 100 pixels, starting at 3; `softness`, 0 to 100 pixels, starting at 0; and `opacity`, 0 to 100 per cent, starting at 100. The numbers can be keyed (D-68) and are held inside their ranges at each frame; the colour cannot. **The rule.** The band's covering at a pixel is the greatest covering the drawing has within the width of it, counted on whole-pixel steps: a step counts when its length is no more than the width, so a width of 1 reaches the four pixels beside a pixel but not its corners, and 2.5 reaches two across and one down but not two and two. A soft edge of the drawing therefore makes a band only as strong as itself past it. The band is then blurred by document 21's Gaussian blur at sigma softness / 3, so the softness is the blur's reach in pixels, and it is the chosen colour at that covering times the opacity, behind the drawing as one picture goes behind another. Width 0 changes nothing, whatever the softness. **The method** is this program's own, modelled on After Effects' Stroke and Photoshop's Stroke layer style set outside; nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017). A positive width grows its bounds by the width, rounded up, and the blur's reach on every side, so the band round the drawing's edge is kept when the drawing is moved (FX-OUTLINE-014); a draft preview scales the width and the softness (D-66). **Not in this decision:** a band inside the drawing's edge or centred on it, a dashed band, a band traced round a mask's path rather than the drawing's pixels, and a band measured by exact distance rather than whole steps, which would round a wide band's corners more smoothly. **Out of range.** A command with a width, a softness or an opacity outside 0 to 100, or a colour not written `#` and six hexadecimal digits, is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one, written or at a key, keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-OUTLINE-015 to 020).

D-119 / Noise / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-26** by the owner's batch message of 2026-09-26, "after this, and listing the 10 recommended effects to build in one batch, proceed with said batch", the ninth of the ten effects the agent listed and recommended (D-111 to D-120). One picture in `verification/B-62a proposal/`. FX-NOISE-001 to 018 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-62. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It gives a drawing film grain: each shown pixel's colour moves a small amount up or down, differently at every pixel, so flat cel colours pick up the texture of film stock. It is `core.noise`, named Noise in the Effects panel. **Settings:** `amount`, 0 to 100, starting at 10; `mode`, the word `mono` or `color`, starting at `mono`; `seed`, 0 to 100000, starting at 0, of which only the whole part counts; and `animate`, the word `on` or `off`, starting at `on`. Amount and seed can be keyed (D-68) and are held inside their ranges at each frame; mode and animate cannot. **The method.** The grain is not drawn from a random source: at each pixel it is a fixed hash (SplitMix64's mixing step) of the seed, the pixel's place in the drawing's own space, the frame and the channel, turned into a number between -1 and 1. So the same file always gives the same grain, a different seed gives a different grain, and a layer that moves carries its grain with it rather than sliding over it. With `animate` on the frame is the composition frame, so the grain changes every frame; with it off the frame counts as 0, so the grain holds still. With `mono` the three channels take the same number, a grey grain; with `color` each takes its own. Each channel of the pixel's straight colour through the sRGB curve moves by `amount / 100 * 0.5` times its number and is held inside 0 and 1, so at 100 a channel can move by up to half, white can only darken and black only lighten. The covering is kept, so a soft edge stays soft, and a pixel that does not show stays as it is. At amount 0 it changes nothing. The method is this program's own, modelled on After Effects' Noise; nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017), with no growth of its bounds and no distance for a draft preview to scale; the grain is one pixel of the drawing. **Not in this decision:** grain larger than a pixel, grain that follows the picture's brightness, After Effects' clipping option (here the result is always held inside 0 and 1), and noise on the covering. **Out of range.** A command with an amount outside 0 to 100, a seed outside 0 to 100000, or a mode or animate other than its two words is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-NOISE-013 to 018).

D-120 / Chromatic aberration / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-26** by the owner's batch message of 2026-09-26, "after this, and listing the 10 recommended effects to build in one batch, proceed with said batch", the tenth of the ten effects the agent listed and recommended (D-111 to D-120). One picture in `verification/B-63a proposal/`. FX-CHROMA-001 to 016 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-63. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It splits a drawing's red and blue apart about a centre, as a cheap lens does: the red is drawn a little larger and the blue a little smaller than the green, so edges away from the centre gain a red fringe on their outer side and a blue one on their inner side, the further out the wider. It is `core.chromatic_aberration`, named Chromatic Aberration in the Effects panel. **Settings:** `amount`, 0 to 100, starting at 3, how many pixels the red and the blue each move at the drawing's corners; and `center`, two numbers, per cent of the drawing's width and height as Radial Blur's centre is, starting at 50, 50, its middle, allowed from -1000 to 1000 so the centre may sit off the drawing. Both can be keyed (D-68) and are held inside their ranges at each frame. **The rule.** With k the amount over half the drawing's diagonal, each pixel takes its red from the point k of the way nearer the centre, its blue from the point k of the way further out, and keeps its own green; each sample is the smooth one between the four nearest pixels, and a sample off the layer reads transparent. Its covering is the largest of the two samples' coverings and its own, so a fringe that falls on an empty pixel shows. Amount 0 changes nothing. **The method** is this program's own, modelled on After Effects' lens effects (the channel offsets of a colour split about a centre); nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017), with the centre in the drawing's own size even after an effect above it has grown the layer. It does not grow the layer: a fringe that would fall past the layer's edge is cut, and a picture against that edge loses its blue there, as FX-CHROMA-001 and 007 show. The amount is a distance, so a draft preview scales it. **Known limits:** the fringe is two colours, red and blue, not a spectrum; over an empty pixel a fringe is pure red or pure blue at the sample's covering, as the green there is the empty pixel's own, which the picture's third panel shows as a strong ring; and past half the drawing's diagonal the red picture turns over through the centre, as FX-CHROMA-005 at frame 4 shows. **Out of range.** A command with an amount outside 0 to 100 or a centre number outside -1000 to 1000 is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-CHROMA-012 to 016).
D-121 / Lens Blur's iris and highlights, as After Effects' Camera Lens Blur has / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-27 by the owner ("2 - accept them all"), with every other decision then proposed (D-167).** It was **PROPOSED on 2026-09-26 by the agent, at the owner's "expand lens blur capability, combine standard with different variations within, like AE CC lens blur does with it's camera blur types"**. One picture in `verification/B-64a proposal/`. FX-LENS-019 to 044 in document 25 are its fixtures; to be built as B-64. **It adds six settings to Lens Blur and changes no existing fixture:** at their start values, and in a file written before them, the rule is D-116's, and FX-LENS-001 to 018 are the same numbers to the byte. **What it does.** A real lens's out-of-focus spot takes the shape of the hole its blades leave, so a bright point opens into a hexagon or a triangle rather than a circle, and bright lights open into bright discs rather than fading into the dark round them. Lens Blur keeps its one card and gains the shape of that hole, its iris, and its highlights. **Settings,** besides D-116's radius and edges: `iris`, the word `circle`, `triangle`, `square`, `pentagon`, `hexagon`, `heptagon`, `octagon`, `nonagon` or `decagon`, starting at `circle`; `roundness`, 0 to 100, starting at 0, how far a polygon is rounded toward the circle; `rotation`, -3600 to 3600 degrees clockwise from up, starting at 0, the iris turned; `aspect`, 0.1 to 10, starting at 1, the iris's width over its height, as an anamorphic lens stretches it, its area kept; `highlight_gain`, 0 to 100, starting at 0; and `highlight_threshold`, 0 to 100 per cent, starting at 100. Every number can be keyed (D-68) and is held inside its range at each frame; the iris word cannot be keyed. **The rule.** The iris is still a set of whole-pixel steps averaged evenly. A polygon of n blades stands on one flat side with its corners at the radius, so a triangle points up and a square is upright; it holds the steps inside it. Roundness mixes the polygon's measure of a step with the circle's, so at 100 it is the circle. The iris is stretched by the aspect, square root of it across and one over that down, then turned by the rotation. A step exactly on the iris's edge counts, with a billionth of a pixel of slack, so every machine counts it the same. Each pixel spreads over the iris, so a single bright pixel becomes the iris's own shape, point up for a triangle. Before the average, a pixel whose brightest channel, taken without its covering, is at or above the threshold has its colour, not its covering, multiplied by 1 plus the gain; after it, a colour past its covering, lit past white, is held at white. With gain 0 nothing is lit. **The method** is this program's own, modelled on After Effects' Camera Lens Blur's Iris Shape, Roundness, Rotation and Aspect Ratio and its Specular Highlights; nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** As D-116. With `transparent` the bounds grow by the radius times the larger of the stretch across and down, rounded up; with `repeat` they do not. A draft preview scales the radius alone. **The card.** An iris list, and a small drawing of the iris beside it; rotation turned on a dial as the other angles are (W-27). **Not in this decision:** a depth map to vary the blur across the picture, the fringe of light After Effects calls diffraction, and a highlight saturation setting. **Known limit:** at a radius under 1 the pixel is still taken alone whatever the aspect, as D-116's. **Out of range.** A command with any setting outside its range, or an iris word not in the list, capitals included, is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-LENS-037 to 044).

D-122 / The batch of ten on the card, each held to 1 level of 255 / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-27 by the owner ("2 - accept them all"), with every other decision then proposed (D-167).** It was **PROPOSED on 2026-09-26 by the agent, at the owner's "now proceed to gpu-accelerate effects if not implemented along with a performance audit all around these new effects"**. D-100 has each effect declare and measure its own tolerance when it moves to the card, and show it in pictures before it is accepted. **The proposal:** Curves, Levels, Hue/Saturation, Gradient, Drop Shadow, Lens Blur (with D-121's iris and highlights), Rim Light, Outline, Noise and Chromatic Aberration each keep compositing's tolerance when they are the last effect of a drawn layer: no channel of any pixel more than 1 level of 255 from the CPU's picture. **How the card does it:** the same rule as the CPU, pixel for pixel, in 32-bit floats: the drawing goes to the card in full precision, as for Bloom (D-104), because a steep Levels or Curves would magnify half precision's rounding. Curves' splines are solved on the CPU and only evaluated on the card. Noise draws the CPU's own numbers, its 64-bit hash worked in pairs of 32-bit words, so the grain is the same grain. Lens Blur keeps its running totals in double precision, as Bloom's streaks do, and adds the CPU's rows of the iris in the CPU's order. Drop Shadow, Rim Light and Outline blur with the CPU's weights in the pass Gaussian Blur already uses, and Outline's band is a greatest-of, which comes out exact. It needs `SHADER_F64`, as B-47 does; a card without it has such frames drawn by the CPU with an Info message. An effect that changes nothing is not sent. **One exception, kept on the CPU:** a Levels whose input white equals its black is a threshold, and a rounding either side of it would move a pixel from black to white, so such a Levels is always drawn by the CPU. **The measurement** is B-65's, over every fixture frame of the ten and the reference shot with each, at Full and Draft. **What it does not change:** exports and fixtures stay on the CPU, byte-exact, and a frame the card cannot draw is drawn by the CPU exactly as before. **If refused:** the ten go back to the CPU, as in P-21, and nothing else moves. **Measured by B-65 on 2026-09-26** (`verification/B-65_gpu_fx_table.md`): 2710 of 2710 checks pass, every fixture frame of the ten and the reference shot with each at Full and Draft within 1 level of 255 and with the same warnings, and the CPU drawing a plan made for the card byte-identical. The worst frame, three Hue/Saturations at Full, has 3.8% of its pixels 1 level apart.

D-123 / Distance Gradation / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-26** by the owner's message of 2026-09-26, "go ahead with the ten", the first of the second batch of ten effects the agent listed and recommended (D-123 to D-132). One picture in `verification/B-66a proposal/`. FX-DISTGRAD-001 to 024 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-66. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It lays shading that fades in from the edge of a drawing's covering, as a cel's shadow or a coloured rim is laid along the inside of its outline in anime finishing: full at the edge, and gone a chosen number of pixels in; or, turned round, gathered in the middle and gone at the edge. It is `core.distance_gradation`, named Distance Gradation in the Effects panel. It touches only the pixels that show, and keeps each one's covering, so the shading never spills past the drawing and a soft edge stays soft. **Settings:** `color`, `#rrggbb` as D-87's, starting at `#6450a0`; `width`, 0 to 1000 pixels, starting at 10, how far in the shading reaches; `opacity`, 0 to 100, starting at 50; `invert`, the word `off` or `on`, starting at `off`; and `blend`, the word `normal`, `multiply`, `screen` or `add`, starting at `multiply`. The width and the opacity can be keyed (D-68) and are held inside their ranges at each frame; the colour and the words cannot. **The rule.** Each pixel that shows finds how far its centre is from the nearest pixel that is out: a pixel of the layer less than half covered, or any pixel past the layer's edge, so a pixel on the layer's edge is one pixel from it, and a pixel that is itself out is none. Its strength is full half a pixel from the edge and falls evenly to nothing `width` pixels further in; `invert` on takes one less that strength. The pixel's own colour is then moved toward the blend of itself and the colour by that strength times the opacity, as Gradient's (D-114) is: the colour itself for `normal`, the two multiplied for `multiply`, the screen of the two for `screen`, the two added for `add`. Width 0 changes nothing, whatever `invert` says. **The method** is this program's own, modelled on OLM's Distance Gradation in spirit (a distance from the covering's edge turned into a strength); nothing is ported. **Naming.** "Distance Gradation" is an OLM plug-in's name, and document 16 says OLM's names are not planned product names: the name is flagged for document 10's naming review before launch. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017), on the layer as it reaches the effect, so an effect above it that grew the layer moves the layer's edge out with it. It does not grow the layer. The width is a distance, so a draft preview scales it. **Known limits:** a pixel is in or out at half covering, so along a soft edge the shading steps where the covering crosses half, and a pixel less than half covered but showing, being itself out, takes the full strength (FX-DISTGRAD-004 shows it); distances are between pixel centres, so on a small drawing the shading goes in steps of about a pixel; a drawing that fills its layer to the edge is shaded along that edge, as the layer's edge counts as out (FX-DISTGRAD-002's column 0 shows it); and `add` is not held below 1, so on a light drawing it can brighten past white. **Out of range.** A command with a width outside 0 to 1000 or an opacity outside 0 to 100, a colour not written `#` and six hexadecimal digits, or an invert or blend other than its words is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-DISTGRAD-018 to 024).

D-124 / Light Rays / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-26** by the owner's message of 2026-09-26, "go ahead with the ten", the second of the second batch of ten effects the agent listed and recommended (D-123 to D-132). One picture in `verification/B-67a proposal/`. FX-RAYS-001 to 024 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-67. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It draws streaks of light from the bright parts of a drawing, away from a chosen point, as light pours round a sun or through the gaps of a window: each bright pixel is smeared outward along the line from the centre through it, and the streaks are added on top of the drawing, tinted by a colour. It is `core.light_rays`, named Light Rays in the Effects panel. **Settings:** `center`, two numbers, per cent of the drawing's width and height as Radial Blur's centre is, starting at 50, 50, its middle, each allowed from -1000 to 1000 so the centre may sit off the drawing; `length`, 0 to 100, starting at 50, how far back toward the centre each pixel gathers light, in per cent of its distance from the centre; `threshold`, 0 to 100, starting at 70, how bright a pixel must be to give light; `intensity`, 0 to 10, starting at 1, how strongly the rays are added; and `color`, `#rrggbb` as D-87's, starting at `#ffffff`, the rays' tint. The four numbers can be keyed (D-68) and are held inside their ranges at each frame; the colour cannot. **The rule.** (1) The light: each pixel that shows and whose brightest channel, in 8-bit steps, is at least the threshold's share of 255, exactly Glow's and Bloom's bright test (D-89); every other pixel gives nothing. (2) The rays: the light through Radial Blur's zoom about the centre with its amount set to the length (D-95 with D-110), so each pixel is the plain average of the light at points on the line from itself back toward the centre, as many points as the path needs, up to 256; with length 0 the rays are the light itself. (3) The rays times the colour and the intensity are added to the drawing's colour, and the rays' covering times the intensity to its covering, which stops at full; the colour is not cut off at white. Intensity 0 changes nothing, and length 0 still adds each bright pixel onto itself. **The method** is this program's own, modelled on After Effects' CC Light Rays in spirit, not claimed to match it, and built from D-89's bright test and D-95's zoom; nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017), with the centre in the drawing's own size even after an effect above it has grown the layer. It does not grow the layer: the rays are cut at the layer's edge, as FX-RAYS-017 shows. Nothing is scaled for a draft preview. **Known limits:** the rays are a smear of the light, not a shadow cast: a dark shape in front of a bright one breaks the light into streaks only because it is not bright itself, as the window bars in the picture do, and a dark pixel the rays pass over is brightened like any other; the rays add covering as well as colour, so a black colour lays a dark smear rather than nothing, as FX-RAYS-009 shows; the bright test reads each pixel's own colour; and a half-covering edge of a bright colour gives light at its own covering. **Out of range.** A command with a length, threshold or intensity outside its range, a centre number outside -1000 to 1000, or a colour that is not `#rrggbb` is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-RAYS-018 to 024).

D-125 / Exposure Flicker / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-26** by the owner's message of 2026-09-26, "go ahead with the ten", the third of the second batch of ten effects the agent listed and recommended (D-123 to D-132). One picture in `verification/B-68a proposal/`. FX-FLICKER-001 to 022 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-68. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It makes a drawing's brightness jitter from frame to frame, as an old film's exposure flickers: on each frame the whole drawing is brightened or darkened by a number of stops, the same for every pixel, different from one frame to the next. It is `core.exposure_flicker`, named Exposure Flicker in the Effects panel. **Settings:** `amount`, 0 to 4 stops, starting at 0.25, the most the brightness may move either way; `hold`, 1 to 100 frames, starting at 1, how many frames each brightness lasts, of which only the whole part counts; and `seed`, 0 to 100000, starting at 0, of which only the whole part counts. All three can be keyed (D-68) and are held inside their ranges at each frame. **The rule.** With the frame's number divided by the hold and rounded down, Noise's fixed hash (D-119) of the seed and that number gives a number between -1 and 1; the stops are the amount times it, and the drawing is then run through Exposure's rule: every colour channel times 2 to the power of the stops, the covering unchanged. So the same file always flickers the same way, a different seed flickers differently, a hold of 2 keeps each brightness for two frames, and at amount 0 nothing changes. A pixel that does not show stays as it is, and a soft edge keeps its covering. **The method** is this program's own, modelled on After Effects' Exposure with a seeded wiggle on its stops; nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017), with no growth of its bounds and nothing for a draft preview to scale. The frame it reads is the composition frame, a hidden value filled in as Noise's is: never saved, and part of what the effect cache keys on. **Known limits:** the brightness jumps from one held value to the next and never glides between them; the whole layer flickers as one, with no part of it brighter than another; and, as Exposure's rule does not clamp, a bright colour pushed up passes white in the working values, which FX-FLICKER-004 shows and the screen then clips. **Out of range.** A command with an amount outside 0 to 4, a hold outside 1 to 100 or a seed outside 0 to 100000 is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-FLICKER-016 to 022).

D-129 / Gradient Map / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-26** by the owner's message of 2026-09-26, "go ahead with the ten", the seventh of the second batch of ten effects the agent listed and recommended (D-123 to D-132). One picture in `verification/B-72a proposal/`. FX-GRADMAP-001 to 023 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-72. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It maps each pixel's brightness to a ramp of three colours: a shadow colour for black, a midtone colour at the midpoint and a highlight colour for white, so a whole cel can be graded into one mood at once, a moonlit night, a sunset, a flashback's sepia. With its starting colours, black, #808080 and white, it turns the picture to grey. It is `core.gradient_map`, named Gradient Map in the Effects panel. It touches only the pixels that show, and keeps each one's covering, so a soft line edge stays soft and takes the same colour as the line. **Settings:** `shadow_color`, `midtone_color` and `highlight_color`, `#rrggbb` as D-87's, starting at `#000000`, `#808080` and `#ffffff`; `midpoint`, 1 to 99, starting at 50, how bright a pixel must be to take the midtone colour; and `amount`, 0 to 100, starting at 100, how far each pixel is moved toward its mapped colour. The midpoint and the amount can be keyed (D-68) and are held inside their ranges at each frame; the colours cannot. **The rule.** Each pixel that shows finds its brightness, from 0 for black to 1 for white: the weighted sum of its red, green and blue in linear light (0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722), turned back to the encoded scale a drawing program shows. Below the midpoint it takes the colour that far between the shadow and midtone colours, above it the colour that far between the midtone and highlight colours, each mixed as the colours are written (encoded values). The pixel's own colour is then moved toward that colour by the amount, as Gradient's `normal` blend does. **The method** is this program's own, modelled on After Effects' Gradient Map (and its Tritone in spirit); nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017). It does not grow the layer, and a draft preview changes nothing, as it has no distances. **Known limits:** three colours only, no free list of colour stops; the brightness weights are fixed; the ramp is two straight runs that meet at the midtone colour, so a smooth shading through the midpoint can show a crease there when the midtone colour is far off the line between the other two; and a saturated colour and a grey of the same brightness take the same colour, so red #c82828 and blue #4060ff map nearly alike (FX-GRADMAP-004). **Out of range.** A command with a midpoint outside 1 to 99, an amount outside 0 to 100, or a colour not written `#` and six hexadecimal digits is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-GRADMAP-017 to 023).

FX-BALANCE-001 to 019 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-73. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It tints a drawing's shadows, midtones and highlights separately, as a colourist cools the darks and warms the lights of a shot: each tone range has its own push up or down on red, green and blue, and each pixel takes the pushes of the ranges its brightness falls in. It is `core.color_balance`, named Color Balance in the Effects panel. It touches only the pixels that show, and keeps each one's covering, so a soft line edge stays soft. **Settings:** `shadows`, `midtones` and `highlights`, three numbers each, red, green and blue, each -100 to 100, all starting at 0, 0, 0. Each of the three can be keyed (D-68) as Radial Blur's centre is, one key holding all three numbers, and each number is held inside its range at each frame. **The rule.** Each pixel that shows reads its colour as it is written (encoded values, 0 to 1) and its brightness from them, the standard weights 0.2126, 0.7152 and 0.0722. A black pixel takes all of the shadows, a white one all of the highlights, and a pixel at half brightness all of the midtones; between black and half it shares the shadows and the midtones in proportion, and between half and white the midtones and the highlights. Each channel is then moved by its share of the three numbers over 200, so 100 moves it half its whole scale, held between 0 and 1, and goes back to linear light at the pixel's own covering. It does not grow the layer, and a draft preview changes nothing, as nothing in it is a distance. **Known limits:** the three ranges meet in straight lines, not After Effects' own curves, so its numbers will not match After Effects' for the same settings; there is no "preserve luminosity" choice, so a push on one channel also changes the pixel's brightness; and a channel already at its end cannot go further, so white takes no push upward and black none downward (FX-BALANCE-003 and 006). **Out of range.** A command with any of the nine numbers outside -100 to 100, or a tone not written as three numbers, is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-BALANCE-015 to 019).

FX-OFFSET-001 to 023 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-74. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It slides a drawing's picture across itself with wrap-around: what leaves one edge comes back in at the opposite edge, so a background drawn to tile can be slid round and round for a looping pan, as a background slide is in anime finishing. It is `core.offset`, named Offset in the Effects panel. **Settings:** `shift`, two numbers, x then y, in pixels, starting at 0, 0, each allowed from -100000 to 100000; positive x slides right and positive y down. It can be keyed (D-68), one key holding both numbers, and is held inside its range at each frame. **The rule.** Each pixel takes the picture from the point `shift` behind it, wrapped round the layer's own edges: a whole-pixel shift moves every pixel exactly, and a shift with a part of a pixel takes the smooth mix of the four nearest pixels, wrapped, as document 21's bilinear sample does. A shift of a whole width or height, or of any number of them, changes nothing, so 100000 across a drawing 16 wide changes nothing and -99999 is the same as 1. Nothing is lost or gained: the picture's total is kept. **The method** is this program's own, modelled on After Effects' Offset (its Shift Center To); nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017). It does not grow the layer, and the wrap goes round the layer as it reaches the effect, the pixels an earlier effect grew included: after a drop shadow that grew the layer two pixels on every side, a drawing 16 wide wraps at 20, as FX-OFFSET-017 shows. The shift is a distance, so a draft preview scales it. **Known limits:** it wraps round the layer, not the composition, so a drawing smaller than the frame slides round inside its own rectangle, and a drawing that was not drawn to tile shows a seam where its edges meet; to tile a drawing exactly, put Offset before any effect that grows the layer; and a shift with a part of a pixel softens the picture a little, as FX-OFFSET-010 shows, so a slide keyed to whole pixels on every frame stays sharp. **Out of range.** A command with a shift number outside -100000 to 100000 is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one, as a constant or at any key, keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-OFFSET-019 to 023).

D-127 / Turbulent Displace / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-26** by the owner's message of 2026-09-26, "go ahead with the ten", the fifth of the second batch of ten effects the agent listed and recommended (D-123 to D-132). FX-TURB-001 to 026 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-70. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It warps a drawing with a smooth, seeded, moving wobble: heat haze over a road, a figure seen through water, a dream's ripple. Each pixel takes the picture from a point pushed a little way off, and neighbouring pixels are pushed alike, so straight lines bend into waves rather than breaking up. It is `core.turbulent_displace`, named Turbulent Displace in the Effects panel. **The name is the owner's choice** over "Heat Haze", and is After Effects' own effect name: it is flagged, with Fractal Noise (D-128), for document 10's pre-launch naming review. **Settings:** `amount`, 0 to 1000, starting at 10, how many pixels a push reaches at most; `size`, 1 to 1000, starting at 60, how many pixels one wave spans; `complexity`, 1 to 8, starting at 2, of which only the whole part counts, how many finer layers of wobble lie on top; `evolution`, -100000 to 100000 degrees, starting at 0; `speed`, -360 to 360 degrees a frame, starting at 20; `seed`, 0 to 100000, starting at 0, of which only the whole part counts; and `edges`, the word `transparent` or `repeat`, starting at `transparent`. Every number can be keyed (D-68) and is held inside its range at each frame; the word cannot. **The rule.** The push at each pixel is the amount times two values of Fractal Noise's field (D-128), one across and one down, taken at the pixel's place in the drawing's own space; the pixel then takes the smooth sample between the four nearest pixels at the pushed point. Evolution moves the field through a third direction, one full turn moving it one wave, and speed adds that many degrees every frame, so with speed not 0 the warp moves from frame to frame. With `transparent` the layer first grows by the amount, rounded up, on every side, so a picture pushed past its edge is kept, and a push that reaches past the picture reads emptiness; with `repeat` it does not grow and a push past the edge reads the nearest edge pixel. Amount 0 changes nothing. **The method** is this program's own, modelled on After Effects' Turbulent Displace in spirit and not claimed to match it; nothing is ported. The same file always gives the same warp, and a layer that moves carries its warp with it. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017), in the drawing's own space even after an effect above it has grown the layer. With `transparent` it grows the layer by the amount rounded up; with `repeat` it does not. The frame it uses is the composition frame, a hidden value filled in as Noise's is, never saved, and the effect cache keys on it. The amount and the size are distances, so a draft preview scales both. **Known limits:** one kind of warp, a push in a noise direction, with none of After Effects' twist, bulge or vertical-only kinds and no pinning of the layer's corners or edges; at the start settings the wave is wider than a small drawing, so a small drawing mostly slides whole (FX-TURB-001), which is the right look on a full frame; and a push at the drawing's edge with `transparent` reads emptiness, so an edge that touches the drawing's border can be eaten in, as FX-TURB-001's first three columns show. **Out of range.** A command with a number outside its range or an edges word other than its two is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-TURB-019 to 026).

D-132 / Light Wrap / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-26** by the owner's message of 2026-09-26, "go ahead with the ten", the tenth of the second batch of ten effects the agent listed and recommended (D-123 to D-132). One picture in `verification/B-75a proposal/`. FX-WRAP-001 to 024 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-75. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It lets the light of what is behind a layer bleed onto the layer's edges, as a bright sky wraps round the outline of a cel laid over it, so the cel sits in the shot instead of looking cut out and pasted on. It is `core.light_wrap`, named Light Wrap in the Effects panel. It is the first effect that reads the layers beneath its own: the owner chose on 2026-09-26 that it reads everything beneath, the frame drawn so far, as an adjustment layer reads it (D-66), rather than one chosen layer. It touches only the pixels the layer covers and keeps each one's covering, so the light never spills past the cel. **Settings:** `width`, 0 to 500, starting at 10, how far in from the edge the light reaches, a distance; `intensity`, 0 to 400 per cent, starting at 100; and `blend`, the word `screen` or `add`, starting at `screen`. The numbers can be keyed (D-68) and are held inside their ranges at each frame; the word cannot. **The rule.** The frame beneath the layer is blurred, and so is the layer's own covering, both by Gaussian Blur at a third of the width, each on the frame's own size. At each pixel the layer covers, the light is the blurred frame beneath times how much of the blurred covering is missing there, times the intensity: much at the edge, where the blurred covering is thin, and little deep inside. That light is screened onto the pixel's own colour (held at white first) or added to it, and the pixel keeps its covering. The layer is then drawn by its opacity and blend mode as usual. With nothing beneath, or intensity 0, nothing changes. Width 0 leaves the blur out, so only a pixel the layer part covers, its soft edge, takes the light, through its uncovered part (FX-WRAP-006). **The method** is this program's own, modelled in spirit on the light wrap compositors use, Nuke's LightWrap node the best known; nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** Not in the layer's own space, an exception to ADR-017 as an adjustment layer's effects are: the layer's other effects, mask, transform and matte run first, in their order, wherever Light Wrap stands in the stack (FX-WRAP-013 and 014 are the same frame); then, when the layer is about to be drawn onto the frame, before its opacity and blend mode, each enabled Light Wrap runs in stack order, in the frame's pixels. Inside a precomposition, what is beneath is that composition's own frame. On an adjustment layer it changes nothing, as that has no drawing of its own (FX-WRAP-015). It does not grow the layer. The width is a distance, so a draft preview scales it. **Known limits:** it reads the whole frame beneath, not one chosen layer, so a dark layer between the cel and a bright background dims the wrap; the blur is cut at the frame's edge, where nothing is beneath, so a wide wrap near the frame's edge, or wider than a small frame, takes less light, as FX-WRAP-003 shows; `add` is not held below 1, so a bright background can light an edge past white (FX-WRAP-007); and as its picture depends on everything drawn beneath the layer, a change to any layer beneath works it again. **Out of range.** A command with a width outside 0 to 500, an intensity outside 0 to 400, or a blend other than its two words is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-WRAP-019 to 024).

D-133 / The second batch of ten on the card, each held to 1 level of 255 / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-27 by the owner ("2 - accept them all"), with every other decision then proposed (D-167).** It was **PROPOSED on 2026-09-26 by the agent**, the step after the second batch that the owner's "go ahead with the ten" set going, as D-122 was for the first ten. D-100 has each effect declare and measure its own tolerance when it moves to the card, and show it in pictures before it is accepted. **The proposal:** Distance Gradation, Light Rays, Exposure Flicker, Vignette, Turbulent Displace, Fractal Noise, Gradient Map, Color Balance and Offset each keep compositing's tolerance when they are the last effect of a drawn layer, and Light Wrap keeps it wherever it is: no channel of any pixel more than 1 level of 255 from the CPU's picture. **How the card does it:** the same rule as the CPU, pixel for pixel, in 32-bit floats, with the drawing sent in full precision as for D-122. Exposure Flicker's flicker, Turbulent Displace's and Fractal Noise's noise are the CPU's own numbers, its 64-bit hash worked in pairs of 32-bit words as Noise's is, so the flicker and the pattern are the same. Distance Gradation measures its distances in whole squared pixels in double precision, which comes out exact. Offset and Turbulent Displace sample in double precision where the CPU does. Light Rays uses the card's bright pass (D-104) and radial blur (B-44) and adds them as the CPU does. **Light Wrap** reads everything beneath its layer, so on the card the frame is laid in order: the layers beneath are laid, then the wrapped layer alone, both are blurred with the CPU's weights, the light is added, and the result is laid with the layer's opacity and blend, as D-132's rule does on the CPU. Until now a frame with a Light Wrap was drawn by the CPU. It needs `SHADER_F64`, as B-65 does; a card without it has such frames drawn by the CPU with an Info message. An effect that changes nothing is not sent. **The measurement** is B-76's, over every fixture frame of the ten and the reference shot with each, at Full and Draft. **What it does not change:** exports and fixtures stay on the CPU, byte-exact, and a frame the card cannot draw is drawn by the CPU exactly as before. **If refused:** the ten go back to the CPU, and nothing else moves. **Measured by B-76 on 2026-09-26** (`verification/B-76_gpu_fx_table.md`): 2560 of 2560 checks pass, every fixture frame of the ten and the reference shot with each at Full and Draft within 1 level of 255 and with the same warnings, and every frame with an adjustment layer drawn by the CPU byte-identical. The worst frame, three Vignettes at Full, has 0.2% of its pixels 1 level apart. On this card Offset first came back empty: a shader function returning four doubles returns zeros, so the shaders return single precision from such functions and widen it where it is used.

D-134 / Invert / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-26** by the owner's message of 2026-09-26, "afterwards, work on 30 more recommended effects for either AE or/and anime/animation related.", the first of the third batch of thirty effects the agent chose and recommended (D-134 to D-163). One picture in `verification/B-77a proposal/`. FX-INVERT-001 to 020 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-77. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It turns a drawing's colours to their opposites, as a photographic negative does: black becomes white, white black, skin a deep blue-green and red a cyan. It can turn one colour channel alone, red, green or blue, leaving the other two exactly as they were, or turn the covering itself, so what showed disappears and what was empty inside the layer turns black. It is `core.invert`, named Invert in the Effects panel. The name is After Effects' own effect name: it is flagged for document 10's pre-launch naming review. **Settings:** `channel`, exactly `rgb`, `red`, `green`, `blue` or `alpha`, starting at `rgb`, not keyable; and `amount`, 0 to 100, starting at 100, how far each value goes toward its opposite: 100 all the way, 50 exactly half way, so every colour meets the middle grey, and 0 not at all. The amount can be keyed (D-68) and is held inside its range at each frame. **The rule.** For `rgb`, `red`, `green` or `blue`, each pixel that shows reads its colour as it is written (encoded values, 0 to 1), moves each chosen channel the amount's share of the way to 1 minus itself, so at 100 an 8-bit value v becomes 255 - v, and goes back to linear light at the pixel's own covering; the channels not chosen, and the covering, are kept exactly. For `alpha`, every pixel of the layer moves its covering the amount's share of the way to 1 minus itself and keeps its own colour, black where it had none. Amount 0 changes nothing. **The method** is this program's own, modelled on After Effects' Invert; nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017). It does not grow the layer, and a draft preview changes nothing, as nothing in it is a distance. With `alpha`, only the layer's own pixels are turned: the composition around the layer stays empty, as FX-INVERT-015 shows. **Known limits:** it inverts the encoded values, as a drawing program does, not linear light, so a mid grey #808080 barely moves (to #7f7f7f) where a linear inversion would lighten it; After Effects' other channel spaces (HLS, YIQ, and its others) are not offered; and `alpha` on a drawing that fills its layer makes it vanish entirely, turning its transparent surroundings into a black card the layer's size, which the picture's fourth panel shows. **Out of range.** A command with an amount outside 0 to 100, or a channel that is not one of the five words exactly as written (capitals are not the word), is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-INVERT-016 to 020).

D-135 / Brightness & Contrast / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-26** by the owner's message of 2026-09-26, "afterwards, work on 30 more recommended effects for either AE or/and anime/animation related.", the second of the third batch of thirty effects the agent chose and recommended (D-134 to D-163). One picture in `verification/B-78a proposal/`. FX-BRICON-001 to 022 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-78. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It lightens or darkens a drawing, and pushes its tones apart from the middle for a punchier picture or draws them together toward it for a flat, washed-out one, the two most asked-for colour knobs, as a finishing pass lifts a dark shot or knocks back a background. It is `core.brightness_contrast`, named Brightness & Contrast in the Effects panel. The name is After Effects' own effect name, flagged for document 10's pre-launch naming review, as D-127's and D-128's are. It touches only the pixels that show, and keeps each one's covering, so a soft line edge stays soft. **Settings:** `brightness`, -150 to 150, starting at 0, how many levels of 255 every channel is lifted (or lowered, below 0); and `contrast`, -100 to 100, starting at 0, how far the tones are pushed apart from half brightness (above 0) or drawn toward it (below 0). Both can be keyed (D-68) and are held inside their ranges at each frame. **The rule.** Each pixel that shows reads its colour as it is written (encoded values, 0 to 1). Contrast first: each channel's distance from half is multiplied by a slope, 1 at contrast 0, falling in a straight line to 0 at -100, so -50 halves every distance and -100 makes every pixel flat mid grey, and rising above 0 as one over one less 0.99 times the contrast over 100, so 50 nearly doubles the distances and 100 multiplies them by 100, turning every channel black or full but those within a level of half. Then brightness over 255 is added to each channel. The result is held between 0 and 1 and goes back to linear light at the pixel's own covering. Both at 0 change nothing. **The method** is this program's own, modelled on After Effects' Brightness & Contrast in spirit and not claimed to match it; nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017). It does not grow the layer, and a draft preview changes nothing, as nothing in it is a distance. **Known limits:** contrast turns about half the scale as it is written, not about the picture's own middle tone, so a dark drawing darkens further with contrast; brightness is a plain lift, so it flattens the lights as they reach white and the darks as they reach black, rather than After Effects' gentler curve, and its numbers will not match After Effects' for the same settings (FX-BRICON-002 to 005); and it works each channel on its own, so strong contrast turns colours toward the pure colours they lean to, as FX-BRICON-009 shows. **Out of range.** A command with a brightness outside -150 to 150 or a contrast outside -100 to 100 is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one, as a constant or at any key, keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-BRICON-017 to 022).

D-136 / Black & White / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-26** by the owner's message of 2026-09-26, "afterwards, work on 30 more recommended effects for either AE or/and anime/animation related.", the third of the third batch of thirty effects the agent chose and recommended (D-134 to D-163). One picture in `verification/B-79a proposal/`. FX-BW-001 to 022 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-79. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It turns a drawing grey, as black-and-white film does, but lets each of six colours decide how light its own grey comes out, as a coloured glass in front of a black-and-white camera does: with a red filter the skin and a red bow come out light and a blue sky dark, with a blue one the other way round. It is `core.black_white`, named Black & White in the Effects panel. **The name is After Effects' own effect name**, flagged for document 10's pre-launch naming review with the rest of the third batch. It touches only the pixels that show, and keeps each one's covering, so a soft line edge stays soft. **Settings:** `reds`, `yellows`, `greens`, `cyans`, `blues` and `magentas`, each -200 to 300, starting at 40, 60, 40, 60, 20 and 80. Each can be keyed (D-68) and is held inside its range at each frame. **The rule.** Each pixel that shows reads its colour as it is written (encoded values, 0 to 1) and orders its three channels from largest to smallest. Its grey starts at the smallest channel; the step from the smallest to the middle one is added in the proportion of the setting for the two largest channels' mixture (red and green: yellows; green and blue: cyans; red and blue: magentas), and the step from the middle to the largest in the proportion of the setting for the largest channel (reds, greens or blues), each number over 100. So a pure colour's grey is its own number over 100 up the written scale (pure red at 40 is 40 per cent of the way up), a colour between two takes a share of each, and a grey, black or white stays exactly as it is whatever the numbers. The grey is held between black and white and goes back to linear light at the pixel's own covering. Where two channels are equal the choice of order makes no difference, so the result changes smoothly with the colour. **The method** is this program's own, modelled on After Effects' Black & White in spirit and not claimed to match it; nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017). It does not grow the layer, and a draft preview changes nothing, as nothing in it is a distance. **Known limits:** no tint choice of its own (Tint or Gradient Map, D-129, placed after it does that); the six colours are fixed at the primaries and their mixtures, with no hue slider between them; the grey is worked in written values, not in light, so the start settings match the drawing's brightness only roughly; and numbers far from the start push many colours to pure black or white, held there, as FX-BW-004, 005 and 011 show. **Out of range.** A command with any of the six numbers outside -200 to 300 is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-BW-017 to 022).

D-137 / Posterize / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-26** by the owner's message of 2026-09-26, "afterwards, work on 30 more recommended effects for either AE or/and anime/animation related.", the fourth of the third batch of thirty effects the agent chose and recommended (D-134 to D-163). One picture in `verification/B-80a proposal/`. FX-POSTER-001 to 018 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-80. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It cuts each of a drawing's colour channels down to a few flat steps, so a smooth shading turns into bands of flat colour: the look of a cel painted in a handful of flat tones, of a screen print in a few inks, or of a stylised title. It is `core.posterize`, named Posterize in the Effects panel. **The name** is After Effects' own effect name: it is flagged, with the third batch's other names modelled on After Effects' effects, for document 10's pre-launch naming review, as D-127's and D-128's are. It touches only the pixels that show, and keeps each one's covering, so a soft line edge stays soft and takes the same steps as the line. **Settings:** `levels`, 2 to 256, starting at 6, of which only the whole part counts: how many steps each of red, green and blue keeps. It can be keyed (D-68), is held inside its range at each frame, and then only its whole part counts, so a keyed change of levels steps from one whole number to the next. **The rule.** Each pixel that shows takes its colour on the encoded scale a drawing program shows, from 0 to 1. Each of its three channels is cut into as many equal parts as the levels, and the channel becomes the step its part stands for, the steps spread evenly from 0 to 1: at levels 2 a channel is either 0 or full, at levels 6 it is one of 0, 51, 102, 153, 204 and 255 (of 255). A value that sits exactly on a boundary between two parts goes to the upper one, as a small lift of 1e-4 before the cut decides; so at levels 256 every 8-bit colour stays exactly as it is. **The method** is this program's own, modelled on After Effects' Posterize in spirit and not claimed to match it; nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017). It does not grow the layer, and a draft preview changes nothing, as it has no distances. **Known limits:** the steps are on the encoded scale, evenly spaced, and the same for all three channels, with no choice of palette and no dither, so a smooth shading shows hard bands, which is the point; the cut is a cliff, so two colours one 8-bit step apart on either side of a boundary land a whole step apart (the greys 127 and 128 at levels 2 turn black and white, FX-POSTER-002), and a gently moving shading can flicker between steps from frame to frame; and levels 255 is not the drawing but lifts every channel a little, as FX-POSTER-006 shows, since only 256 steps match an 8-bit value's. **Out of range.** A command with levels outside 2 to 256 is refused with a sentence; the range is on the number as written, before its whole part is taken, so 256.5 is refused; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-POSTER-013 to 018).

D-138 / Threshold / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-26** by the owner's message of 2026-09-26, "afterwards, work on 30 more recommended effects for either AE or/and anime/animation related.", the fifth of the third batch of thirty effects the agent chose and recommended (D-134 to D-163). One picture in `verification/B-81a proposal/`. FX-THRESH-001 to 019 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-81. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It turns a drawing into pure black and pure white, as a copy machine or a line test does: every pixel that shows and is at least as bright as a chosen level turns white, and every darker one turns black. It splits a cel into its light and its shadow, or cleans a scanned pencil drawing down to its lines. It is `core.threshold`, named Threshold in the Effects panel. It touches only the pixels that show, and keeps each one's covering, so a soft line edge stays soft, in black or in white. **Settings:** `level`, 0 to 255, starting at 128, the brightness a pixel must reach to turn white, on the 0 to 255 scale of an 8-bit colour. It can be keyed (D-68) and is held inside its range at each frame. **The rule.** Each pixel that shows reads its colour as it is written (encoded values, 0 to 1) and its brightness from them, the standard weights 0.2126, 0.7152 and 0.0722, so a pure green counts as far brighter than a pure red, and a pure blue as darker than either. It turns white when 255 times that brightness, plus one ten-thousandth, is at least the level, and black otherwise; the ten-thousandth makes a grey sitting exactly on the level, such as #808080 at the starting 128, turn white the same way in the build as in the reference. The pixel's covering is kept. At level 0 every pixel that shows turns white; at 255 only white stays white. **The method** is this program's own, modelled on After Effects' Threshold; nothing is ported. **The name** is After Effects' own effect name: it is flagged, with the rest of the third batch, for document 10's pre-launch naming review, as D-127's and D-128's are. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017). It does not grow the layer, and a draft preview changes nothing, as nothing in it is a distance. **Known limits:** the choice is a cliff, a pixel either side of the level turning the other way entirely, so a smooth gradient becomes a hard edge and a slowly keyed level makes pixels flip one frame to the next (FX-THRESH-011); a soft edge keeps its covering but not its colour, so an antialiased line edge turns wholly black or wholly white at half covering (FX-THRESH-001); only black and white, no chosen colours (Tint or Gradient Map after it gives those); and a pixel within a hair of the level could in principle be decided differently by the build's single precision, which the fixtures avoid by design. **Out of range.** A command with a level outside 0 to 255, or not a number, is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-THRESH-015 to 019).

D-164 / A number written as a word in the third batch's fixtures / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-27 by the owner ("2 - accept them all"), with every other decision then proposed (D-167).** It was **PROPOSED on 2026-09-26 by the agent**, found while building B-81. Three of the third batch's fixtures, FX-THRESH-019, FX-LWIPE-032 and FX-BLINDS-026, write a setting that must be a number as a word (`"level": "128"`, `"completion": "50"`) and expect the file to open, the effect kept as written and left out of every frame with `EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID`. Every effect built before them does otherwise: a number written as a word is a fault in the file's shape, and the file is refused on opening with `PROJECT_SCHEMA_INVALID`, as every B-table's "The file" section checks. The fixtures were written by the agent in the same night's work and nobody chose the difference. **The proposal:** keep the rule every effect has, and have those three cases expect the file refused. The builds B-81, B-98 and B-100 follow the existing rule, and their tables show each of the three as a row "in dispute" that checks the file is refused, not as a passing fixture. The fixtures themselves are not changed until this is decided. **If refused** (the owner prefers such a file to open with the effect kept and skipped): the reading of a number setting changes for every effect, not only these three, since one effect opening a file another would refuse is worse than either rule; every B-table's shape rows for a number written as a word change with it.

D-139 / Channel Mixer / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-26** by the owner's message of 2026-09-26, "afterwards, work on 30 more recommended effects for either AE or/and anime/animation related.", the sixth of the third batch of thirty effects the agent chose and recommended (D-134 to D-163). One picture in `verification/B-82a proposal/`. FX-MIXER-001 to 022 in document 25 are its fixtures; built as B-82. **It adds one effect and changes no existing fixture.** **What it does.** It rebuilds each of a drawing's red, green and blue from a mix of all three: a colourist swaps two channels for an alien sky, takes one away, turns the picture to grey by chosen weights, or makes a negative. It is `core.channel_mixer`, named Channel Mixer in the Effects panel. The name is After Effects' own effect name: it is flagged for document 10's pre-launch naming review, as D-127's and D-128's are. **Settings:** `red`, `green` and `blue`, four numbers each, how much of the pixel's red, of its green and of its blue go into that channel, and a constant added to it, each -200 to 200, in per cent of the channel's whole scale; they start at 100, 0, 0, 0, then 0, 100, 0, 0 and 0, 0, 100, 0, each channel from itself alone. Each of the three can be keyed (D-68) as Color Balance's tones are, one key holding all four numbers, and each number is held inside its range at each frame. `monochrome`, the word `off` or `on`, starting at `off`, not keyed. **The rule.** Each pixel that shows reads its colour as it is written (encoded values, 0 to 1). Each channel becomes its row's first number times the red, plus the second times the green, plus the third times the blue, plus the constant, all over 100, held between 0 and 1, and goes back to linear light at the pixel's own covering. With monochrome on every channel uses the red row, so the picture turns grey by its weights, and the green and blue rows are not used. The rows as they start with monochrome off change nothing; with monochrome on they give each pixel the grey of its own red. **The method** is this program's own, modelled on After Effects' Channel Mixer in spirit and not claimed to match it; nothing is ported. **Where it runs.** On a drawing's own pixels before its transform (ADR-017). It does not grow the layer, and a draft preview changes nothing, as nothing in it is a distance. **Known limits:** it works on the colour as it is written, not in linear light, so a mix of 50 and 50 is a mix of the written values; weights that do not add up to 100 change the greys too (FX-MIXER-004); a channel pushed past its end is held there, so detail beyond it is lost (FX-MIXER-011); and there is no "preserve luminosity" choice. **Out of range.** A command with any number outside -200 to 200, a row not written as four numbers, or a monochrome word other than its two is refused with a sentence; a file that holds one keeps the effect as written and leaves it out of every frame with EFFECT_PARAMETER_INVALID, as D-46 does (FX-MIXER-017 to 022).

D-140 / Vibrance / **ACCEPTED on 2026-09-26** by the owner's message of 2026-09-26, "afterwards, work on 30 more recommended effects for either AE or/and anime/animation related.", the seventh of the third batch of thirty effects the agent chose and recommended (D-134 to D-163). One picture in `verification/B-83a proposal/`.
